Smriti Irani returns to BJP core team: Why it matters ahead of 2027 UP polls
Smriti Irani, one of the BJP's most recognisable campaigners, had remained outside the party's central organisational structure after losing the 2024 Lok Sabha election from Amethi. Her return now places a high-visibility political face alongside experienced organisational strategists such as Sunil Bansal, Vinod Tawde, Biplab Kumar Deb and Satish Poonia.
The BJP’s decision to bring back former Union minister Smriti Irani as a national general secretary is more than an organisational reshuffle. Her return to the party’s core team under president Nitin Nabin comes at a time when the BJP is preparing for a crucial round of state elections, with Uttar Pradesh emerging as the biggest political test on the horizon.
Irani, one of the BJP’s most recognisable campaigners, had remained outside the party’s central organisational structure after losing the 2024 Lok Sabha election from Amethi. Her return now places a high-visibility political face alongside experienced organisational strategists such as Sunil Bansal, Vinod Tawde, Biplab Kumar Deb and Satish Poonia.
The biggest reason could be Uttar Pradesh. The BJP is preparing for the 2027 Assembly election in the state, where it faces the challenge of rebuilding momentum after the setbacks of the 2024 Lok Sabha polls.
NOT A STRANGER TO UTTAR PRADESH
Irani's political identity remains closely linked to Uttar Pradesh. Her defining electoral moment came in 2019 when she defeated then Congress president Rahul Gandhi in Amethi by over 55,120 votes. Gandhi had represented the constituency since 2004.
That victory transformed Irani into one of the BJP’s most celebrated campaigners and established her as a leader capable of taking on the Congress’s top leadership.
Her relationship with Amethi, however, goes back to 2014. Although she lost that election, Irani continued to work in the constituency, visiting villages, building relationships with local workers and strengthening the BJP’s organisation.
She lost Amethi again in 2024, this time to Congress candidate Kishori Lal Sharma by more than 1.67 lakh votes. But the defeat did not erase her wider political value to the BJP.
As national general secretary, Irani can now be deployed beyond a single constituency. Her role is likely to involve campaigning, coordination with state units, organisational mobilisation and helping the party manage electoral battles.
A DIFFERENT KIND OF ORGANISATIONAL LEADER
Irani brings something different to the BJP’s new general secretary team. Bansal is associated with building the BJP’s electoral organisation in Uttar Pradesh, while Tawde and Poonia bring extensive experience of managing state units and organisational affairs.
Irani, by contrast, is a high-visibility campaigner with a strong public profile. That combination could be particularly useful in Uttar Pradesh, where the BJP will need both organisational machinery and a strong political narrative.
Her return therefore appears to be about putting a familiar and combative face back into the BJP’s election campaign at a critical time.
A WOMAN LEADER WITH YOUTH LEADER
Another factor behind Irani’s return is the BJP’s focus on women voters. Women have emerged as an important electoral constituency for the party, with welfare programmes and direct-benefit schemes helping the BJP build a strong base among female voters.
Irani gives the party a prominent woman leader who can carry that message directly to voters. She also has a strong social media presence, with around 1.6 million followers on Instagram, giving her access to a younger and digitally engaged audience.
Her communication style is another asset. Irani has built a reputation as a sharp and combative speaker who can take on political opponents directly. That makes her particularly suited to a campaign environment where the BJP will be fighting for both votes and the political narrative.
MORE THAN A COMEBACK
Irani’s return also carries a message for the BJP’s cadre. She rose rapidly through the party’s ranks, became a prominent face of the Modi government and emerged as one of its most effective political communicators.
Her appointment as the only woman among the eight national general secretaries also stands out in Nitin Nabin’s new team.
The BJP has simultaneously increased women’s representation across its national organisation, with six women among the 13 national vice presidents.
Long story short: the appointment puts a proven campaigner, a prominent woman leader and a politician with a strong Uttar Pradesh connection back at the centre of the BJP’s national election machinery.

If the BRS is a party that provides ‘justice to one family’ alone, the Congress has become a party of ‘justice for brothers’, while the BJP is the only party that truly stands for ‘justice for the people’, asserted Telangana BJP president N. Ramchander Rao on Monday.

Telangana currently has 36 government institutions offering more than 4,400 MBBS seats, but only four of its government medical colleges have found a place among the top 144 government medical institutions in the country in the latest International Institutional Ranking Framework (IIRF) 2026 rankings.
The rankings, which assess higher education institutions across several academic and institutional parameters, have placed Gandhi Medical College, Secunderabad as the highest-ranked government medical college from Telangana at 43rd position. Osmania Medical College, Hyderabad, followed at 52nd position, while Kakatiya Medical College, Warangal, was ranked 60th. Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS), Adilabad, was placed much lower at 139th position.
At the national level, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, secured the first position among government medical institutions.
Private colleges: 18 Telangana institutions in top 187
The representation of Telangana was considerably higher in the private medical colleges category. Of the 187 private medical colleges included in the IIRF list, 18 institutions from Telangana featured in the rankings. The State currently has 29 private medical colleges, collectively offering around 5,850 MBBS seats.
The top position in the private medical colleges category was secured by Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore.
The rankings therefore present a contrasting picture for the State. While its established government institutions such as Gandhi Medical College and Osmania Medical College feature within the upper half of the national government medical colleges list, a large number of newer government medical colleges established during the State’s recent expansion of medical education do not feature among the 144 ranked institutions.
Three Telangana dental colleges make the cut
Telangana also had three institutions in the IIRF rankings for dental colleges. Army College of Dental Sciences, Secunderabad, was the highest-ranked Telangana institution at 33rd position. It was followed by Malla Reddy Institute of Dental Sciences, Hyderabad, at 53rd and Malla Reddy Dental College for Women, Hyderabad, at 64th.
Maulana Azad Institute of Dental Sciences, New Delhi, secured the first position in the dental category.
What does IIRF measure?
The IIRF rankings are based on nine broad parameters, together accounting for 100% of the assessment. These include academic reputation; graduate outcomes and employability; research outcomes; demand ratio and student profile; employer reputation and international outlook; wellbeing and institutional development; peer perception and alumni feedback; public perception and data verification; and impact and value addition.
The methodology is intended to assess institutions beyond academic performance alone, taking into account factors such as research, employability, institutional development, stakeholder perception and the broader impact of an institution.

CEO who went viral for firing 900 employees on Zoom before Christmas is now mad that he got fired
Vishal Garg, the CEO and founder of Better.com, was let go and replaced by a hedge fund manager who joined the company’s board only a week earlier, according to a report
The CEO of Better Homes & Finance — who notoriously laid off 900 employees on a company Zoom call before Christmas in 2021 — says he feels tricked, as he was just fired and replaced.
Vishal Garg, who made headlines in 2021 for the cruel firings of hundreds of employees at the digital mortgage company, was let go from Better, which he founded and led as CEO, on August 3, CNN reported.
Hedge fund manager Daniel Lewis was then immediately named as the company’s interim CEO — even though he had only been brought onto the board a week earlier. Within that week, Garg says that Lewis convinced the board to oust him. Garg says Lewis then convinced the board to name him as the new CEO.
“He hoodwinked me,” Garg told CNN. “He said he liked the company’s strategy. He praised us on X and used that to get on our board and win our confidences.”
The digital mortgage company had seen numerous setbacks over the years under Garg’s leadership — excluding the catastrophic layoffs, which gained nationwide attention and resulted in the website being flooded with negative reviews.
While Better held an $8 million valuation during the COVID-19 pandemic amidst a refinancing boom and low interest rates, it is now valued at only $300 million, according to the report.
Despite the troubles, Garg said he was on the precipice of turning fortunes around for the company. While sales dropped from $1.5 billion in 2021 to $70 million in 2023, this year Better is on pace to deliver $200 million in sales, Garg told the outlet.
That is in part because of its AI models, which it uses to help quickly process mortgages — something that would’ve taken dozens of employees several days to do just years ago.
“We’re winning. We’ve tripled loan volume. We’re close to profitability,” Garg said. “We were at the 5-yard line after taking the ball all the way down the field from the other side.”
Despite his best efforts, Garg said he feels that Lewis convinced the company’s board to get rid of him.
“It’s not about me. I care about delivering savings to people and helping them live the American Dream. So when shareholders said, ‘You need to take a back seat,’ I complied,” Garg said.
Garg added: “I suspect he always wanted to become CEO. The board made a mistake.”
Investors may agree with Garg’s read on the situation. The company’s stock had fallen 45 percent since Lewis was named as the new CEO.
In the days since, Garg retained a lawyer to try to help him win back his job. He sent a letter to the board on Monday demanding he be reinstated as CEO.
Garg says he will work for $1 a year until Better returns to profitability. Once that goal is reached, he says he will leave the role as CEO.
“It’s an acknowledgement that I’ve been doing this for 10 years, but execution hasn’t been perfect,” he said. “I hope it gets resolved. I think the future still remains very bright for Better.”

When Edward Warchocki speaks with you, he sounds like a regular guy. “Not super intelligent, but very emotional, very easy to make friends with,” says Bartosz Idzik, the person who created him. But when he doesn’t talk, it’s harder to forget what Warchocki really is: a 4-foot-tall humanoid robot that’s wandering the city streets of Poland.
Six months ago, Idzik and his friend Radosław Grzelaczyk had the idea of buying a humanoid robot from China. They named it “Edward Warchocki” after Grzelaczyk’s dog Eddie and the Polish word for growling, “warczeć,” but also because it sounds like a passable name for a Pole. The first few days they took Edward out, it couldn’t speak, and people were clearly scared of it. Then Idzik, a software developer, wired Edward to a large language model that made it capable of having live conversations in Polish.
“When he started to talk, people loved him. Without talking, it’s just a 40-kilogram machine,” Idzik says.
Edward soon made lots of friends. It visited the Polish parliament and talked to politicians, hiked up mountains and waded in the lake, and was jokingly arrested by the police. In April, a video of it chasing away wild boars in Warsaw, armed with a backpack and a Rolex, went viral worldwide. By now, Edward has over 1 million followers and 4 billion views across social media.
In 2026, you must have seen at least one of these humanoid influencers vibing around the world. There’s “Rizzbot,” which wears a cowboy hat and flirts with passersby on the streets of Austin; “Bart Robot,” which was breakdancing with Knicks fans in New York, celebrating the team’s historic championship; and the “Brickell Clanker,” which changed into different jerseys to party with World Cup fans after each game.
But unless you’ve been paying close attention, you probably haven’t realized these robots are all the same model: Unitree G1, one of the most available and affordable humanoid robots on the global market today, made by a Chinese company that’s leading the robotics industry. The G1 is about the size of a child, with a hollowed-out face with a ring of blue light and light-gray limbs made of aluminum. It’s going on America’s Got Talent, showing off kung fu, having boxing matches, parkouring, dancing at concerts, running with kids, cooking (but failing), streaming with Kai Cenat, begging for money, dating itself, being ordained as a monk in Japan and Korea, and praying at a mosque in Dubai.
An anonymous shitposter on X put it: “This clanker is lit as fuck!”
Unitree will go public on the Chinese stock market in about two weeks. Its financial disclosure tells how popular the company’s products are: Unlike most robot companies whose products are still being tested in labs, more than half of Unitree’s 2025 revenue came from delivering humanoid robots to real customers. It shipped 5,511 humanoids in 2025 at an average price of less than $25,000 each. And 43 percent of all sales came from outside China. The company also became profitable for the first time last year.
“We tested a lot of humanoids, and the G1 was the best for its purpose,” Idzik says. “We are used to China copying other countries, but from the perspective of humanoids, other people should copy China. ”
Despite its commercial success, the company and its robots are often the subject of intense doubts. Sure, they can perform clout-seeking, crowd-pleasing tasks, but can they hold down a traditional job contributing to the economy, like working on an assembly line or cleaning a house? When will Unitree G1 get a real job?
Buying It in the US
Jake Cooperstein, a 24-year-old who lives in Miami, says he was inspired by Edward and other accounts to create a humanoid influencer of his own. In January, he visited the warehouse of a robotics shop in New York and tested the Unitree G1 robot. He was impressed by how easy it was to operate. The next day, he secured an order and paid the deposit.
On Unitree’s website, a basic G1 robot is priced at $13,500, but that’s before any tariff, shipping, and taxes. A US distributor lists the robot at about $19,000 instead. Cooperstein was not satisfied with that, though. The most basic version doesn’t come with more sophisticated parts like dextrous hands and is prohibited from modification. He instead chose the U5 variation that’s designed for educational buyers. It has more parts and better customization but sits at the price of $66,000.
Cooperstein named his G1 robot the “Brickell Clanker,” after the downtown Miami neighborhood, and started taking it out in public to interact with people.
Brickell Clanker got its big break by attending the World Cup games after-parties this summer, changing into different jerseys for Argentina, Brazil, and the US. Today, Cooperstein makes money mostly by charging a fee to bring Brickell Clanker to influencer parties, nightclubs, and corporate events. Rates range from $800 to $1,200 an hour, depending on what the robot needs to do.
Cooperstein recently got another robot: a Unitree R1. At almost one-third the base price of the G1, this faster, lighter model is Unitree’s attempt to make humanoids even more affordable. He named the new robot the “Lil Clanker.”
It’s unclear whether he’ll be able to keep buying Unitree’s robots. In July, the US Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on new Chinese-made humanoid robots. The models that had cleared approvals—like Unitree G1 and R1—are theoretically still allowed, but no one knows for sure. What’s certain is that when Unitree releases its next generation of humanoid robots, it won’t be able to sell them to the US. Unitree didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Hardware and Software Limits
In Europe, Edward Warchocki faces fewer threats. Idzik says MERA Robotics, the company he cofounded with Grzelaczyk, now has a fleet of 20 humanoid robots, most of them Unitree G1. Every robot in Poland shares the personality of Edward, but they also have some in the Middle East and Southeast Asia operating as different influencers.
While the LLM can enable the robots to converse freely, when it comes to physical movement they’re still under a lot of constraints. Both Idzik and the Cooperstein say that when they bring the robots out now, they are teleoperating the robots most of the time. Theoretically, the Unitree G1 should be able to move around in the physical environment by itself, but they are worried of a malfunction possibly hurting a bystander, creating a safety hazard.
The G1 robot that Cooperstein got came with about 20 gestures and 15 dance moves built in. Beyond that, it takes some technical knowledge to program new movements. For example, he taught the Brickell Clanker to move its arms in a way that simulates the signature “Viking Row” gesture done by Norwegian soccer fans this year.
Cooperstein still remembers the first day he took Brickell Clanker to the World Cup fan festival. Hundreds of people, including the press, circled the humanoid and cheered it on as it danced. “Nobody knows that it's me controlling it. It seems like I'm blending in with the crowd. I'm just staring out and looking at everybody,” he says, “and I'm like, ‘holy shit, this is the future.’”

22 more bodies recovered in Zimbabwe ferry disaster, bringing death toll to 68, police say
Police say 18 children are among the nearly 70 people killed this week when an overloaded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe
HARARE, Zimbabwe -- Eighteen children were among the nearly 70 people killed when an overloaded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe this week, police said Saturday after rescuers recovered more bodies.
The ferry capsized in strong waves Tuesday and police said 22 more bodies were recovered since then, bringing the death toll to 68.
The aging ferry was traveling from Kariba town to rural and fishing communities in the country's northwest, where roads are damaged and public transportation is scarce. Authorities have not said how many people were aboard or how many remain missing.
Estimates have put the number of passengers as high as 153, while authorities say the ferry’s capacity is 90. Zimbabwe’s disaster management agency has said 77 people were rescued.

Authorities initially said the number of children aboard was unknown because those below ticketing age were not included in passenger estimates. A police list released later showed that 16 of the child victims were aged 10 or younger, with the youngest just 1.
Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, created by damming the mighty Zambezi River in the late 1950s and early 1960s. It stretches more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) and is up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.
Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with their border running through its middle.

Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat accident in Zimbabwe, taking the death toll to 68, police said on Saturday.
The ferry capsized on Tuesday on Lake Kariba, on the border with Zambia. An investigation has suggested it was overloaded when it went over during heavy winds.
Eighteen children were among the people killed, Zimbabwe’s police said, in what is believed to be the country’s deadliest such disaster.
Most of the passengers are believed to be villagers and fish traders who lived around the lake.
Officials said the vessel was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.
Lt Col Joseph Muchechesi, commander of the boat regiment involved in the search operation, said: “So far today we have managed to take 22 bodies. We are confident that we will manage to retrieve all the bodies.”
The civil protection unit said on Wednesday that 77 people had been rescued.
Hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in the lakeside town of Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives and loved ones.
A public memorial service was held in Kariba, nearly 280km (175 miles) north-west of the capital Harare, on Thursday before the burials started.
Survivors said they pleaded with the ferry driver to turn back as the vessel had begun taking on water soon after departing.
Chance Siyamavhu, 45, told the Agence France-Presse: “Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top.
“When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the lifejackets but most of them did not even know how to use them.
“Most people could not make it.”
Lake Kariba is the world’s largest manmade lake by volume. It stretches more than 200km (124 miles) and is up to 40km (25 miles) wide in places.
It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people.
In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.
On the Zimbabwean side, five passengers drowned in a 2021 incident.

Justin Blinder lost his job two weeks before the Covid-19 pandemic hit in 2020. To pay his rent, he turned to delivery services, riding his bicycle across New York City to deliver food. As he went, he noticed the disparities in where the food items went. Which order of Nomé sushi went where and how much people tipped.
“The city started to feel much more economically and psychologically disparate,” Blinder tells WIRED. “It really changed so much on a block-by-block level. These inequalities and demographic differences were happening in such close proximity.”
That experience has morphed into an art-project gadget called Ground Truth that Blinder hopes will raise awareness about the housing affordability crisis in New York City and beyond by making a Citi Bike—one of the ever-present ebike rental options across the city—harder to ride through places where it’s harder to live.
Blinder, a Brooklyn artist and contractor at Meta, received a $10,000 grant for the project from a Brooklyn arts organization called Idle Hands.
Ground Truth is a box that will trigger the brakes on the Lyft-owned bicycle, adding more resistance to the pedals when riding through rent-burdened neighborhoods, where people living in those areas spend more than 30 percent of their income on rent. Ride past an economically well-off block, and the bike is easier to pedal. Going past a block where rent takes the bulk of the households’ incomes can slow the bike down to a crawl.
There are two versions, one that can work on a regular bicycle and one built specifically for Citi Bikes.
The box mounts on the bike’s fork and is then attached to the front brake line. A battery-powered GPS component tracks the bike’s location. As it moves, the location is cross-referenced with household economic data from the US Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, stored on the device. When the bike passes a block the dataset says has a higher percentage of rent insecurity, the microcontroller triggers a small motor that applies the brake to add resistance, and the bike gets physically harder to pedal.
Blinder is also the creator of the Covid-inspired Pandemic Pulse, an app that used real time Covid statistics to change the brightness of your device’s screen. The screen would darken whenever data showed infections growing, and then black out briefly whenever a death was recorded. As with Ground Truth, Blinder says the goal of these projects is to help people understand large datasets in a more tactile way.
“It’s really trying to make the way we traditionally visualize a lot of big data more tangible and embodied,” he says. “Create something a bit more confrontational and try to force people to consider how they traditionally look at data.”
Blinder says the device is not a working product or something other people will be able to use. (Likely for legal reasons, as you can’t just change how a rideshare electric bicycle drives.) But he has ridden about 35 miles or so, filming the experience as Ground Truth changes its resistance in different communities.
He hopes the project will also call attention to the rising cost of renting a Citi Bike. The service has raised its prices for the past five years in a row.
“The price has just become so astronomical that it felt like this really nice connective tissue in the affordability crisis, connecting all of those different elements,” Blinder says. “It’s really thinking about how affordability changes throughout the city on a block-by-block basis and how this system could allow people to experience that.”

Jharkhand student protests began on 25 July 2026 over alleged irregularities in the 14th JPSC Preliminary and JSSC-CGL examinations, including allegations of OMR tampering. Led by student leader Devendra Nath Mahto, protesters have demanded cancellation of the exams and an independent CBI probe. On 10 August 2026, thousands of students marched towards the Jharkhand Assembly, where police used lathi charges and water cannons. The government has since agreed to cancel three JPSC examinations, but students continue to demand a CBI probe into the alleged irregularities. As of 14 August 2026, the protests have entered their 21st day, with Mahto continuing his hunger strike and political support for the movement growing (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) claiming to show Abhijeet Dipke arriving in Jharkhand and participating in the student protests. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke reaching Jharkhand and participating in the student protests.
Fact: The viral video does not show Abhijeet Dipke participating in the Jharkhand student protests. It actually shows him attending a CJP demonstration at Jantar Mantar in Delhi on 6 June 2026. While Dipke has supported the Jharkhand protests, he had not travelled to Ranchi at the time of writing this article. A CJP delegation, however, visited Ranchi to support the students. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A Google keyword search found no reports confirming that CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke travelled to Jharkhand or joined the student protests. Instead, multiple reports (here, here) stated that he expressed verbal support for the protests but did not physically join them, saying he did not want to hijack the movement led by Devendra Nath Mahto. We also found reports that a CJP delegation travelled to Ranchi to support students protesting the JPSC and JSSC examinations.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to an X post by Deccan Herald dated 06 June 2026, featuring screenshots containing the same visuals as the viral video. The post was captioned, “‘We are not afraid’: CJP founder Deepak, who is leading the movement to remove Dharmendra Pradhan, has a message for the government.”
This photo was also used in a report published by Deccan Herald on 6 June 2026. According to the report, a crowd of students, young professionals, and activists gathered at Jantar Mantar in Delhi for a CJP demonstration led by CJP founder Abhijit Dipke, who had arrived from the United States earlier that day. The photo caption reads, “Founder of CJP during the protest”
Abhijeet Dipke reposted an X post by Jharkhand student protest leader Devendra Nath Mahato on 11 August 2026. The post mentioned a video call between Mahato and Dipke, during which Dipke expressed his support for the ongoing student protests in Ranchi.
To sum up, this viral video does not show CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke reaching Jharkhand or participating in the student protests.

Family stranded at sea for 16 hours after jet ski capsized in Thailand
- Published
A French family was left stranded at sea for more than 16 hours overnight after their rented jet ski capsized off the coast of Thailand.
A 50-year-old father and his young sons were left "pale" and "exhausted after swallowing a lot of seawater" before being rescued, local government official Amorn Chomchoey told AFP.
All three were taken to hospital for checks but were discharged shortly afterwards, Chomchoey said.
The father had rented the jet ski for a 45-minute ride on Koh Samui, one of Thailand's most popular islands for tourists, at around 17:00 local time (10:00 GMT) on Thursday, the Bangkok Post reports.
Rescuers were alerted after the jet ski was not returned at the agreed time.
People used speedboats and more jet skis to comb the waters surrounding Koh Samui and towards the nearby island of Koh Phangan searching for the family, the Bangkok Post reports.
Search efforts had to be suspended overnight before the family were found still drifting at sea the following day, Thai media report.
The father and sons were found by rescuers at around 10:00 local time on Friday, according to AFP.
The father told authorities that rough waves had struck the jet ski and caused the engine to stop towards the end of the rental period, the Bangkok Post reports.
Footage of the rescue shows one of the boys sat on the top of the front of the jet ski while the rest of the vehicle is submerged beneath choppy waves.
His father can be seen waving at rescuers as he floats nearby. Both of them are wearing life jackets.
English-language news site Nation Thailand reports that the boys' mother and older sister had been waiting on the beach when the trio were brought back to safety.
The family has remained in Thailand and continued their holiday, officials told AFP.

Uganda team manager has 'no idea' why boxers have disappeared
- Published
The team manager for the Ugandan Commonwealth Games team has told BBC Scotland News he has no idea why four boxers with the team have vanished.
Two men and two women who competed for Uganda at the Games failed to turn up for their scheduled flights home and have since turned off their mobile phones.
Media reports in Uganda, external suggested the four may be looking to seek asylum, but Uganda's chef de mission Godwin Kayangwe said he hoped the athletes would return home before their visas expire in October.
Police say inquiries are ongoing into a number of Commonwealth athletes who have failed to turn up for homeward flights, but it is understood little can be done until the existing visas expire.
The four boxers - Ibrahim Kemis, 20, Nuhu Batte, 22, Emily Nakalema, 32 and Angel Katushabe, 21 - were due to fly back to Uganda on Tuesday.
Kayangwe said he has no idea why they have disappeared but suspects they are "probably still in Glasgow or somewhere in Europe."
"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back.
"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.
"Their visas are still valid until October so hopefully, probably, they will come back to their country."
Asked why the athletes might be looking to seek asylum, the team manager said he didn't know.
"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that] - I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."
Sports media site NBS Sports said it had spoken to one of the four missing boxers, who claimed the athletes intended to seek asylum and continue their boxing careers in a country they believed offered better training facilities and opportunities than their homeland.
The boxer was also said to have appealed to Ugandans for understanding and asked not to be judged for the decision.
Kayangwe said the matter was now with the Ugandan high commission who will liaise with the authorities in Scotland.
He added that he had a simple message to the missing athletes.
"My message is pretty clear, observe the law and make sure the visa does not expire while you are still here. Come back to Uganda and and they can probably come back to Europe whenever they want."
He added he hoped the boxers would make the "right decision" and return to Uganda.
Pakistan Today also reported, external that the boxer Qudrat Ullah had not joined the rest of his team-mates in flying home to Pakistan, and that he was not found in his room when officials went to search for him.

Lenskart’s recent results for the first quarter (Q1) of the financial year 2026-27 (FY27) suggest the company is entering a new phase. For years, the listed eyewear brand’s strategy revolved around opening more stores, building its brands and bringing more Indians into organised eyewear. Now, after years of investing in stores, manufacturing, technology and acquisitions, Lenskart wants a bang for its buck. Its Q1 numbers testify to this shift. The listed eyewear brand’s revenue rose 34% year-on-year (YoY) in the June quarter, while net profit jumped 182% to ₹228 Cr. EBITDA grew 61%, and the consolidated product margin exceeded 70% for the first time. India remained the core growth driver, with revenue up 30.7% and same-store sales growth of 18.3%, while international revenue rose 38%. The margin improvement suggests that Lenskart has begun to get more out of the infrastructure it has built over the past few years. However, as Lenskart gets bigger, maintaining same-store growth, customer satisfaction and returns on the capital invested in stores, technology and manufacturing will become more important than simply adding locations. Lenskart Wants To Own Both Ends Of Eyewear Market Lenskart estimates that 78 Cr Indians currently need vision correction, a number that could rise to 94 Cr by FY30. The company has spent years building a business around affordable, mass-market eyewear, but management now says it underestimated how quickly its existing customers would premiumise. The opportunity is visible in the products Lenskart is adding at the upper end. The company defines premium lenses broadly as products above roughly ₹3,500. On frames, it considers products above ₹5,000 to be premium. Brands such as John Jacobs, Meller and newer partnerships are intended to give Lenskart greater exposure to this segment. At the other end, Lenskart has finally cracked a ₹500 eyewear proposition through its Hustlr Plus offering. This may sound like a contradiction: why pursue both premiumisation and ultra-low pricing? Because the company is attempting to turn its retail network into a house of brands rather than a single-price-point retailer. The ₹500 offering is designed to bring new consumers into the market, while premium brands allow existing customers to trade up. Management says it spent years working on the economics of the ₹500 product, with manufacturing scale, logistics optimisation and an omnichannel customer-acquisition model making the proposition viable. Brokerages also seem bullish. Jefferies sees the ₹500 offering as evidence that Lenskart can move further down the price curve without giving up its premiumisation story. Similarly, Macquarie flagged the combination of “strong volume growth”, premiumisation and the ₹500 entry point as key positives. International Moving From Experiment To Growth Engine For years, Lenskart’s international business was one of the biggest questions looming over the company. That equation has begun to change. International revenue increased 38% in Q1, or about 29% on a constant-currency basis. The segment’s product margin reached 77.1%, while eyewear units rose 37.6% and transacting customers increased 27.8%. Importantly, this growth came with only 16 net new stores. That combination suggests that Lenskart is not yet dependent on aggressive international store additions to grow. The company is applying the same basic playbook it developed in India: increase eye tests, improve store productivity, integrate the supply chain, raise product margins and then accelerate store expansion once the operating model is sufficiently mature. The company said in the earnings call that different countries are at different points on that curve. Thailand and the Middle East are still closer to the early stages of the India model, while mature markets such as Singapore and Japan are showing stronger economics. Japan is particularly interesting. Lenskart says the market has high eyewear penetration, but consumers are increasingly moving from traditional opticians toward consumer brands. That gives the company an opportunity even where there is little scope to create demand through first-time eyewear adoption. The acquisition strategy is also becoming more important. Meller, which Lenskart acquired at roughly $35 Mn, is now tracking toward $170 Mn+ in revenue, according to management. The company also highlighted Owndays as an important Asian eyewear brand and is integrating its supply chain more deeply with brands such as Owndays and Meller. But international expansion will require more than transplanting the Indian formula. Lenskart needs to manage different consumer preferences, competitive structures, labour markets and brand identities. The company is therefore investing in GeoIQ and advancing geoanalytics capabilities to replicate the data-driven store-selection model it uses in India. The Next Phase Of Lenskart’s Growth Lenskart’s next challenge is not finding demand. It is scaling the operating model without compromising customer experience or store economics. The company is adding stores rapidly, increasing eye tests and expanding internationally, but each of these moves puts more pressure on optometry, logistics, technology and talent. Lenskart is also increasing in-house production to improve supply-chain control and reduce import and currency exposure. That investment can strengthen margins, but it also raises the importance of generating adequate returns on the capital being deployed. The same tension applies internationally. Lenskart is preparing to accelerate store additions in markets where technology integration and unit economics have matured, but the company has been clear that expansion will follow operational readiness. The ultimate test for Lenskart’s next phase is not whether it can open more stores, but whether it can make a much larger network more productive. Its investments in AI eye testing, remote optometry, manufacturing and data-led store selection are designed to do exactly that. A new document attempting to resuscitate a floundering global plastics treaty suggests that negotiations are trending in a less ambitious direction, a leading scientific expert said.
Talks to strike the world's first treaty addressing humanity's ever-growing tide of plastic pollution fell apart in August 2025 after opposition from oil-producing nations.
The first public document since that collapse was released quietly on the weekend, but quickly came under stinging criticism from environmental groups.
While it resembles a new draft text, chairman of the talks Julio Cordano of Chile emphasised it was "an informal reference document and does not constitute a negotiated or agreed text".
Cordano noted the document took a "balanced approach", with subjects where "views remain divergent" put into brackets.
Richard Thompson, a British marine biologist who coined the term microplastics, told AFP the document was extremely similar to the draft text that was rejected a year ago.
"If anything, it's even slightly weaker," added Thompson, a researcher at Plymouth University who has served as an independent scientific observer to the talks.
Others were more scathing.
"The text cuts the international legal effort to address plastic pollution off at the knees, delivering a text that fails not only future generations, but present ones," the Center for International Environmental Law's David Azoulay said in a statement on Monday.
Once-in-a-planet opportunity
Negotiators from 185 countries have struggled to find common ground between two broad groups.
A majority of nations have called for ambitious, legally binding measures to curb humanity's production of plastic, which is expected to triple by 2060.
However a smaller bloc of mostly oil-producing states -- including Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Russia -- have pushed back against such restrictions, seeking to focus more narrowly on waste management.
Thompson suggested that rising pressure to reduce carbon emissions was leading some oil-producers to seek "an alternative market for growth" by making plastic, which is derived from petroleum.
Research published in The Lancet last year estimates that the many health problems caused by plastic pollution costs the world $1.5 trillion a year.
Thompson also expressed concern that independent scientific observers including himself had been excluded from offering expert advice to negotiators.
"That creates unnecessary suspicion," he said.
Calling the treaty "a once-in-a-planet opportunity," Thompson said he saw "no point... in agreeing on something that is too weak to deliver."
Chairman Cordano said an updated version of the "aid to negotiations" will be prepared after the next round of informal talks in Bangkok from September 27 to 30.
Formal negotiations, hosted by the UN Environment Programme, are then scheduled for March 2027.

Kharif crops' productivity at risk as monsoon trough shifts, widespread regional variations
Soybean, maize, paddy and other kharif crops are now entering the growth stages that determine final yields with an erratic monsoon in tow.
After pulling India back from a near 40% rainfall deficit at the end of June, the southwest monsoon is losing momentum again. The all-India rainfall deficit remained stuck at 12% as of August 13 despite widespread showers in the first half of August, and forecasts suggest rainfall could weaken further through the month.
Soybean, maize, paddy and other kharif crops are now entering the growth stages that determine final yields, and experts say the next fortnight could decide whether the uneven monsoon dents productivity.
The sowing season has virtually ended. Agriculture ministry data show kharif crops were sown over an area about 2% lower than a year earlier as of August 14 — rice acreage down 3.7%, tur and maize by 4% each, cotton by 1% and sugarcane by 0.5%. With little room left for additional planting, this year’s harvest will depend on yields, and on whether crops get adequate moisture through August and September.
IMD predictions amid continuous showers
The national rainfall deficit has barely moved in a fortnight — from 13% below the long period average (LPA) on July 31 to 12% by August 13 — even as many parts of the country received regular showers this month.
In its July 31 long-range forecast, the IMD had projected below-normal rainfall for both August and September, estimating August rainfall at 94% of its long period average of 254.9 mm, with the first half of the month broadly normal before activity weakened later. Its August 13 extended-range forecast reinforces that outlook: near-normal rainfall from August 13-19, turning normal to below normal during August 20-26 as the monsoon trough shifts north again.

Mahesh Palawat, vice president at Skymet Weather, said the first half of August has prevented the rainfall deficit from worsening but has not delivered the widespread soaking rainfall needed to significantly improve the seasonal balance. “We expected some recovery during the first half of August, but substantial rainfall has been missing. Daily rainfall has remained close to the daily long period average… We now expect this to increase slightly after August 15 as the monsoon trough shifts towards the Himalayan foothills...,” he told HT.
The all-India deficit conceals sharp regional variation.
Rainfall deficits across the country
As of August 13, central India had almost erased its rainfall deficit, at just 1% below normal. Northwest India remained 11% below normal and the south peninsula 20% below average. East and northeast India saw the sharpest shortfall, still 27% below the long period average. Several agricultural states lag well behind normal: Bihar is down 39%, East Uttar Pradesh and Punjab 31% each, Jharkhand 25%, and the Haryana-Chandigarh-Delhi subdivision and West Uttar Pradesh around 11%. In the south, Karnataka is down over 21%, Kerala 22%, and parts of Andhra Pradesh over 30%.
IMD data show 40 of India’s top 50 rice-producing districts are running rainfall deficits — as are 21 of the top 25 soybean districts, 18 of the top 21 tur districts and 16 of the top 20 maize districts.
Also Read I Monsoon woes: Potholes on Sherpur road safety hazard; Ludhiana residents see red
Impact on kharif crops
Bhashkar Dubey, Assistant Professor and Agriculture Expert at KIT College, Prayagraj, said the district-level numbers matter more than the all-India deficit. “The biggest concern for kharif crops at this stage is not merely the cumulative rainfall deficit, but the uneven distribution of rainfall, prolonged dry spells and moisture availability during the crop’s critical growth stages,” he said.
Dubey said the 2026 monsoon shows why seasonal totals alone often fail to explain agricultural outcomes. “One or two days of heavy rain cannot compensate for a seasonal rainfall deficit. If heavy rainfall is followed by a long dry spell, soil moisture declines rapidly. This year, some districts have experienced flooding while others continue to struggle with rainfall deficiency and prolonged dry spells.”
Crops are now entering the stages that determine final output. Soybean is particularly at risk, and continued moisture stress through late August could hurt flowering, pod formation and grain filling, reducing yields, Dubey said.
Dubey said most rice-producing districts are rainfall deficient, though irrigation could cushion production in several regions. Rainfed and upland paddy remain vulnerable if dry conditions persist during tillering, panicle initiation, flowering and grain filling. Tur, though relatively drought tolerant, could lose flowers and pods if moisture stress extends into its reproductive stage.
Also Read I Weather Bee: Dry second week of August erased monsoon gains from the first week
Rainfed maize is vulnerable during tasselling, silking and grain filling; cotton faces risk from both dry spells and waterlogging. Dr Vishwas Chitale, Fellow at the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), said this year’s monsoon reflects a longer-term shift — the monsoon is becoming more erratic, not simply wetter or drier.
CEEW’s assessment of four decades of rainfall data shows 55% of India’s tehsils received over 10% higher southwest monsoon rainfall in the past decade compared with the 1982-2011 baseline, while 11% received over 10% less, concentrated across the Indo-Gangetic plains, the northeast and the Himalayan region.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Japan is considering establishing a dedicated agency to support retired Self-Defense Forces personnel and their families as early as fiscal 2027, in an initiative championed by Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi.
The defense minister launched an internal review on the issue in June, instructing officials to examine ways to expand existing assistance and a centralized command tower to oversee it. The Defense Ministry is said to be looking to include related expenses in its fiscal 2027 budget request, expected at the end of this month.
Possible areas for expansion include improving the social standing of veterans’ families, reviewing the structure of post-retirement benefits, assisting wounded personnel and supporting their reintegration into society.
“We need to create an environment in which retired SDF personnel and their families can live out their lives with pride and their heads held high,” Koizumi told a news conference in June after setting up a special panel on the issue.
Support for ex-SDF personnel is currently divided among several ministry departments, without a central body responsible for coordinating policy or providing retired members and their families with a single point of contact.
The proposed body, tentatively called the “retired SDF personnel and family support agency,” would bring those functions together. It is expected to serve as a one-stop consultation center overseeing veterans’ transition to civilian life.
Status as an agency will allow the new organization to be headed by a commissioner, potentially strengthening its ability to coordinate with other government bodies and helping secure funding on a more stable basis.
The initiative is part of Koizumi’s broader push to improve the treatment of SDF recruits during and after their service. By offering more reliable support after retirement, the ministry hopes to make a career in uniform more attractive as it struggles to recruit and retain personnel.
As Japan grapples with a severe demographic crisis, some analysts expect the SDF to shrink by as much as 10% to 15% over the coming decade, even after Koizumi announced in June that the SDF recruited over 11,000 personnel in fiscal 2025, up 14.9% from the previous year.
In terms of models for the new agency, the ministry is looking overseas. The United States, Australia and South Korea, for instance, all have dedicated institutions that assist veterans with healthcare, employment, housing and other critical necessities.

New Delhi, Aug 17: The CPI(M) demanded on Monday that the National Testing Agency (NTA) and the National Education Policy (NEP), 2020, be scrapped, saying errors in three UGC-NET papers have once again exposed the "entrenched rot" in the country's education system.
In a statement issued here, the party's Politburo said the latest errors have exposed the NTA's "abject incompetence" in conducting examinations and reiterated its demand for scrapping the agency as well as the NEP, which it described as the "root cause of the decay in the education system".
"This disgraceful episode has once again exposed the entrenched rot in India's education system and lays bare the NTA's abject incompetence to hold these examinations," the CPI(M) said.
The party alleged that instead of addressing the consequences of the NEP, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its affiliates are targeting those who question the education system.
"Deplorably, instead of remedying the NEP's disastrous consequences, the BJP and its affiliates target those who question the system," it said, while condemning the killing of Janab Mafik, father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) volunteer Shaik Abdul Hafeez, in West Bengal. Mafik died after he was allegedly assaulted at his residence after his son visited a school to record infrastructural gaps.
The NTA on Sunday announced a retest for three papers -- English, Commerce and Sociology -- of the UGC-NET that was held in June following complaints of several errors in these papers.
The English paper will be held from 9 am to 12 noon on September 9, while the Commerce paper will be conducted the same day from 3 pm to 6 pm.
The Sociology re-test will be held from 9 am to 12 noon on September 10.
The NTA conducted the UGC-NET 2026 from June 22 to June 30 across 87 subjects for the award of Junior Research Fellowship (JRF), eligibility for assistant professor and admission to PhD programmes.
In a public notice, the agency said it had received several complaints about multiple errors in the question papers of the three subjects and formed a committee to look into these issues.

Vande Mataram row: Amit Shah attacks Sonia Gandhi, Congress hits back, cases filed
The development came days after Parliament passed a bill that makes any insult to the national song a punishable offence.
The controversy surrounding Congress leader Sonia Gandhi’s alleged objection to the singing of the entire Vande Mataram song during the party’s Independence day celebrations snowballed into a full-blown political feud on Sunday, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) staging protests across the country and registering complaints against the senior opposition leader.
The Congress has denied the allegation that attempts were made by Sonia to stop the singing of the full version of the national song at the AICC headquarters on Saturday. The party said Sonia was only asking for a chair for Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge as he was standing for a while.
The development came days after Parliament passed a bill that makes any insult to the national song a punishable offence. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, was passed by a voice vote in the Lok Sabha on July 30, a day after it was approved by the Rajya Sabha. The law grants status to Vande Mataram on par with national anthem Jana Gana Mana.

Shah targets Congress
Deep Dive
The controversy broke out on Saturday when BJP national general secretary (organisation) B L Santhosh shared a video of the Congress’s event on X. "Mother, son and national president (of the Congress) seem to be upset by the rendering of full Vande Mataram,” he wrote on the micro-blogging site.
On Sunday, Union home minister Amit Shah said the Vande Mataram song was sung at the Red Fort and all other places where flag hoisting was held after 80 years of Independence.
"Thousands of people faced bullets and lathis and were jailed for singing Vande Mataram," he said, referring to the use of the revolutionary slogan during the freedom struggle. "We all saw it on television. Sonia ji, 140 crore (people) are watching you. The people of the country will never forgive you for your sin... If there is any shame left, you should fold your hands and apologise to Bankim Babu's immortal spirit and the people," he added.
The Vande Mataram song was written by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee.
Also Read | Complaint filed against Sonia, Rahul Gandhi over disrespect to Vande Mataram
Shah was addressing a public event at Chittorgarh, Rajasthan, when he made the remarks. He alleged the Congress had forgotten 'Vande Mataram' due to vote-bank politics.
At a press conference in the national capital, BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said the alleged opposition to the Vande Mataram song pointed towards a mindset of a "dimagi Naxal ecosystem".
"Can any patriot, can any Indian who believes in the Constitution of India, respects the Tricolour of India, respects India's freedom fighters and believes in India's sovereignty and integrity, ever get angry at the invocation of Vande Mataram on Independence Day?" he said.
He also said the Congress government in Kerala crossed all limits by completely removing Vande Mataram from the Independence Day celebrations.
Bankim Chandra’s descendant joins protest
BJP MLA Sumitro Chatterjee, a fifth-generation direct descendant of Bankim Chandra, sought an “unconditional apology” from Sonia.
In a letter to the Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson, the MLA from Naihati in West Bengal said the incident had deeply hurt the sentiments of the people of the eastern state, and appealed to her to introspect.
West Bengal CM attacks Congress
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari also said the incident had deeply offended the people of the state, where Bankim Chandra is revered as "Sahitya Samrat".
"Yesterday was Independence Day. During the event at the Congress headquarters in Delhi, when Vande Mataram was being sung, Sonia Gandhi expressed her displeasure at singing the full version. The entire country witnessed this on live telecast," Adhikari told reporters in Kolkata.
He accused the Congress leadership of trying to explain away the episode and said video footage would establish what happened. "As Chief Minister, I feel that insulting Vande Mataram is an insult to Bankim Chandra himself. I strongly condemn this," he said.
Congress refutes allegation
The Congress denied the BJP's allegation that Sonia showed disrespect to the national song or attempted to stop the singing of its full version.
The party maintained that there was no attempt to interrupt the rendition and that Sonia was only asking for a chair for Kharge, who had been standing for some time.
Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh slammed Shah as someone who insulted B R Ambedkar on the floor of the Rajya Sabha on December 17, 2024, and who belongs to an ideology that did not see fit to unfurl the Tricolour at its organisation's headquarters till January 2002.
"A man who insulted Dr Ambedkar on the floor of the Rajya Sabha on Dec 17, 2024. A man who belongs to an ideology that did not see fit to unfurl the tiranga at its headquarters till Jan 2002. A man who orchestrated the Delhi Police's brutalities on peacefully protesting youth,” he said on X.
“Such a man is now demanding an apology from the Congress to divert attention away from the real issues of the day and away from the colossal failures of his and his Sahib's," he added.
Congress's media and publicity department head Pawan Khera said when lathis rained down for chanting "Vande Mataram", it was the Congress that had sounded the bugle of freedom through this song. "At that time, people associated with the Sangh either fled with their tails tucked between their legs or wagged their tails to please their British masters," he said.
Several Congress leaders also shared on social media Ramesh's speech in the Rajya Sabha on December 10, 2025, during a debate marking 150 years of Vande Mataram. Participating in the debate, Ramesh had accused the BJP of distorting history and insulting freedom fighters who sacrificed their lives for the country.
Complaints filed, protests held across country
Multiple protests broke out and complaints were registered against Sonia across the country on Sunday.
A complaint was filed with the Delhi Police seeking registration of an FIR against Sonia and Rahul Gandhi over alleged obstruction during the singing of Vande Mataram. The complaint, filed by an advocate, was submitted at the IP Estate police station on August 16.
The complaint alleged that Sonia made gestures after the initial portion of the National Song had been sung, which the complainant claimed appeared to indicate an objection to its continuation. It also referred to a video in which Rahul is allegedly heard saying, "We are not singing Vande Mataram."
In Bengaluru, the BJP Yuva Morcha (youth wing) lodged a complaint at the Malleshwaram police station regarding the alleged insult and sought legal action. The Yuva Morcha also staged a protest near BJP state headquarters in the Karnataka capital.
In the police complaint, the Yuva Morcha said the song played an important role in the freedom struggle and is presently the national song of India. It is required by the law of our land to be accorded the same respect as our national anthem, "Jana Gana Mana”, they said.
The BJP also held a protest outside the Congress office in Srinagar. The party’s West Bengal unit held protest rallies in Kolkata and Siliguri.
In Manipur, more than 50 BJP workers, holding the national flag and posters of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, raised slogans and played the song on loudspeakers outside the Congress Bhavan.

For decades, Snopes has kept tabs on popular rumors regarding Albert Einstein, the German-born physicist most famous for developing his theory of relativity.
We've looked into multiple quotes attributed to Einstein, such as that he once said, "The only thing more dangerous than ignorance is arrogance," and that he purportedly said, "Two things are infinite: The universe and human stupidity; and I'm not sure about the universe."
We've also fact-checked images — for example, one showing Einstein seemingly bicycling away from an atomic bomb explosion and another allegedly showing him playing the electric guitar.
Decades after his death, we continue to analyze the parts of his life less memorialized, such as his personal philosophical beliefs and whether he married his cousin.
Here are 20 of our Einstein-related stories over the years:

When Soundgarden Wrote “Black Hole Sun,” they may have inadvertently been onto something.
In a new paper in Nature, scientists have chronicled a “black hole star” that’s the size of our solar system and glows bright red in the depth of space. The findings are based on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, which continues to change how astronomers think about the cosmos.
Researchers focused on some of the most distant observable phenomena in the universe, which appear to be something like a star in disguise. Based on the light they emit, they appear to share some characteristics with giant stars, but astronomers suspect they are actually black holes shrouded in an extraordinarily dense and luminous gas.
These hypothetical objects have been dubbed black hole stars, and the new research, published Wednesday, lays out the case for them.
The signal that’s at the center of the study comes from a time when the universe was just 660 million years old. (It's now almost 14 billion years old.) In the JWST images, the object appears as one of the many bright, reddish spots that the telescope has found in the early universe.
From a distance of billions of light-years, this phenomenon appears to be a gigantic star. But the object, known as MoM-BH*-1, has a few curious properties. It emits about 100 billion times more energy than any star could produce through nuclear fusion, according to the team. Even for the era in which it formed—during the early universe—it is an extremely bright object.
Furthermore, part of its light abruptly disappears. Stars can produce a similar signal when their atmospheres absorb certain wavelengths, but in MoM-BH*-1, the effect is too intense to be explained as normal star behavior. Researchers believe that an enormous amount of extremely dense gas is absorbing that light.
These clues led scientists to the black hole star hypothesis. At the center of MoM-BH*-1, there would be a black hole devouring matter and releasing enormous amounts of energy. Surrounding it, a massive gas envelope. The energy would pass through that gas before escaping into space and, in the process, would acquire some of the characteristics we would normally expect to find in starlight.
The hypothesis could help address another mystery uncovered by the JWST. The telescope finds, with surprising frequency, small red spots in the early universe whose origins remain uncertain. They don’t fit neatly into the usual categories of objects in deep space. Scientists have put forward a number of explanations, including that they’re compact galaxies teeming with stars, black holes hidden by dust, and systems completely different from those we observe in the present-day universe.
Black hole stars are also among these possibilities. MoM-BH*-1 is particularly interesting for this area of research because, unlike other red spots, its black hole appears to almost completely obscure the surrounding galaxy.
“Every little red dot is consistent with being a black hole star, embedded in a generic early galaxy. But what is special about MoM-BH*-1 is that the black hole star is essentially completely outshining its surrounding host galaxy, such that we’re seeing pure black hole star light,” Rohan Naidu, the study’s lead author who performed the work while at MIT, says in a press release.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

“We’re all gonna make it, brah!”
That was the aspirational rallying cry of Aziz Shavershian, better known by his online alias, Zyzz. Once the shy and skinny son of Kurdish parents who struggled to find his place in Sydney, Australia, where the family had moved from Russia, he’d thrown himself wholeheartedly into fitness, spending hours at the gym every day and frequenting the infamous Bodybuilding.com and 4chan forums.
In time, the teenager’s chiseled physique gave him the confidence to develop an online persona that had little in common with the gentle and goofy kid that his friends and family knew. This would be Zyzz, a brash raver who strutted, mugged, danced, and flexed shirtless in front of his webcam while asking if viewers were “mirin’” (that is, admiring his body) and exhorting other men to chase their self-improvement goals. By 2010, his videos had made him an Australian celebrity with fans around the globe.
And as of August 2011, he was dead in Thailand, at the age of 22.
Shavershian’s brief and tragic life is the basis of a new documentary, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz, now available on Apple TV and Prime Video. But this keenly nuanced film is more than the familiar tale of an ambitious youth who pursued fame at all costs. It also reckons with the digital forces that could produce a person like Zyzz in the first place, and how his preternatural instincts for navigating a brand-new media ecosystem anticipated an entire generation of masculinity influencers.
Depending on your perspective, Zyzz can be regarded as the original “looksmaxxer”—though the term had yet to be coined—or one of the earliest forefathers of the manosphere as we know it today.
“I really see this as a cautionary tale,” Poster Boy’s director, Selina Miles, tells WIRED. She notes that Shavershian’s meteoric rise and untimely death left a huge impression on Australian millennials, and that his legend continues to reverberate today. “He had his transformation, and his story has really resonated with a lot of people,” she says. “We have to stay curious as to why. Why has he had this impact on men?”
Through a mixture of Zyzz’s archival content and interviews with close friends as well as his older brother, Said Shavershian—a professional bodybuilder to this day—the documentary circles the question of his outsized appeal during a key shift in human communications. At that moment, few imagined YouTube (launched in 2005, when he was 16) or Facebook (first available to him the following year) as a means to notoriety, let alone financial success. Indeed, Zyzz’s earliest videos amount to little more than a kid playing around in his bedroom; later, he and his pals experimented with showing off their abs and biceps at music festivals and nightlife hot spots, hoping for reactions of any kind.
While Zyzz promoted values of inclusion and mutual support for men looking to become the best version of themselves, he also began to feed off those who insulted him, online and off: “U mad?” and “Come at me brah” were two of his recurring catchphrases. He understood sooner than most how controversy drove clicks, and even maintained fake social accounts to amplify the war between himself and the haters. “He made this page on Facebook that was, like, ‘10,000 likes and I'll bash Zyzz,’” Miles says, describing an incident that didn’t make it into the documentary’s final cut. “When the page was doing well, he switched the name of it to be promotion for his protein brand.”
His rhetoric turned homophobic and misogynist, contemptuous of anyone who had not optimized their physical form. A 2010 post on his Facebook page read: “id rather be dead than ‘normal.’”
By then, we learn from the film, Zyzz had more followers on the platform than the prime minister of Australia at the time.
Behind the bravado, however, Zyzz seemed psychologically unprepared for the limelight. In addition to using steroids to sculpt his Renaissance-worthy physique (he and the fitness personalities in his orbit were known as the “Aesthetics Crew”), he took Xanax to deal with the stress and paranoia that came with being mobbed in public, where he was also frequently menaced by young men looking for a fight.
And while acolytes copied his basic workout routines, his own methods grew ever more extreme. In one video, he bragged about obtaining clenbuterol, a prescription drug used to treat asthma in horses, prized by bodybuilders as a supposedly performance-enhancing substance despite the likelihood of dangerous cardiovascular side effects in humans.
Today, manosphere streamers and podcasters can make millions hawking supplements and classes to vulnerable young men looking to take charge of their life in one way or another. Zyzz, Miles says, was “right on the cusp” of that economy, reportedly making about $20,000 in the last three months of his life, which would now be considered a drop in the bucket by major creators. “It makes you realize how much has changed, because you look at how it works today, and it's extraordinary, it's just a gigantic pyramid scheme,” she says.
Poster Boy leaves it up to the viewer to decide the extent to which Zyzz served as a template for the likes of misogynist influencer Andrew Tate, who flashes onscreen in one sequence. (He and his brother, Tristan Tate, are currently fighting extradition from the US to the UK on charges of rape and sex trafficking that their attorney has claimed are without merit.) Setting aside some provocative aspects of behavior, Zyzz did not appear to preach from a place of nihilism or cynicism, and he had a genuine community.
“Aziz did have friends, and I think that male friendship is one of the beautiful themes of this story,” Miles says, referring to the members of the Aesthetics Crew who sat for interviews and remain in touch today. She wonders if they collectively make the case that a currently voguish explanation for radicalization among men, the so-called male loneliness epidemic, “might not be the right term for what we're actually seeing.” In the end, she notes, it was Zyzz who isolated himself from this network as they sought to help him.
Zyzz traveled alone to Thailand in July 2011, having told each of his closest friends that he was traveling with another one of them. After his death, Thai authorities revealed that he purchased a wide variety of pharmaceutical drugs and underwent multiple facial surgeries while in the country. Those who went to identify his body upon its return to Australia recount how they could barely recognize him due to those procedures.
The exact cause of Shavershian’s death was never made public until Poster Boy disclosed the findings of his toxicology report: acute respiratory failure brought on by a combination of morphine, cocaine, and benzodiazepines.
Perhaps it was unavoidable that Zyzz would be mythologized as a martyr for the manosphere. The closing credits of the film show a montage of tattoos in his memory. His brother Said, who runs a fitness brand, sells T-shirts with illustrations of both of their faces and a zeitgeisty, looksmaxxing slogan that would have made little sense 15 years ago: “Mog Them All.” (He continues to follow Zyzz’s playbook when it comes to courting controversy, too, and is shown recording a podcast in which he argues that there is “no such thing as toxic masculinity.”)
But Miles would like viewers to take different lessons from what happened to Shavershian as he evolved into Zyzz, fracturing his real identity in the process of building up the kind of facade that is all too common in the influencer age he prefigured.
“This was this persona that he created, and he felt that it was separate from who he really was, that it was OK to take risks,” Miles says. “It was so successful, and it did kind of take over his life.” Whatever good intentions and ideals he may have had, the incentives of the algorithm “corrupted those, and changed him as a person,” she says.
Yet his formula has clearly endured. There are still a lot of young men who want to hear “that you can be the master of your own universe, you can have some control over your fate, and you can be who you wanna be,” Miles says. “More than ever, men are seeking that sense of hope. And Zyzz kind of gave that to them.”
