It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

Ukraine energy company says its facilities seriously damaged after 13 Russian strikes
Ukraine’s state energy company says Russia has attacked its facilities 13 times over the past week, with nearly 300 attacks this year
KYIV, Ukraine -- Russia attacked facilities of Ukraine’s Naftogaz Group 13 times over the past week and has targeted its premises almost 300 times since the start of the year, the state energy company said Monday.
Russia has repeatedly battered the Ukrainian power grid since its all-out invasion more than four years ago. Moscow hopes to sap Ukraine’s will to fight by denying civilians light, heating and running water during the bitter winter months.
Ukrainian officials, who say Russia is “weaponizing winter,” fear Moscow will pursue its campaign through the coming winter, too.
Russian drones and missiles struck facilities in several regions of the country, with one asset hit multiple times during the week, Naftogaz said, reporting serious damage to equipment and production capacity. No employees were hurt in the attacks, the company said.
With troops largely bogged down by drones and robots along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (780-mile) front line, both Russia and Ukraine are expanding their aerial campaigns and devising new long-range weapons.
Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russia killed seven people, while four civilians died in Ukraine after strikes by Moscow’s forces, officials said Monday as they collated overnight attacks.
Ukraine depended heavily on foreign military aid after Russia’s full-scale invasion of February 2022 but has gradually increased its domestically produced firepower, firing a salvo of more than 800 long-range drones at Russia on Sunday.
Ukraine also has successfully targeted depots owned by Wildberries, Russia’s main online retailer, as far as 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from Ukraine’s border.
Russian forces have increasingly hit apartment blocks, ports, schools and hospitals, among other urban targets, killing close to 17,000 civilians, according to the United Nations. The death toll of 437 Ukrainian civilians in July was 70% higher than the same month in 2025, it said last week, as Russia's barrages intensified.
Russia has exploited Ukraine’s severe shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, which are the only way of countering ballistic missiles.
But Kyiv is swiftly innovating, with Ukraine now developing its own ballistic missile to hit back at Russia and working with European countries on developing more anti-ballistic air defenses.

NEW YORK — Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday to federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, admitting matter-of-factly that he trailed the executive to an investor conference in 2024 and gunned him down on a New York City street.
Mangione, 28, said he even used a ruse to glean information about the event, contacting the health insurance company ahead of time under the guise of being an investor at a multibillion-dollar firm.
“On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024, I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan, and he died,” Mangione told the court as Thompson’s wife, Paulette, took several deep breaths and repeatedly wiped tears from her eyes. A supporter put an arm around the wife and held her tight.
Mangione is set for sentencing Dec. 18. When U.S. District Judge Margaret M. Garnett asked whether he understood that he could spend the rest of his life in prison, Mangione answered neutrally: “Yes.”
Mangione entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death. Mangione’s lawyers could now seek to have his separate New York state murder case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.
Surveillance video of the ambush showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson, 50, from behind. Police say “delay,” “deny” and “depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims. That detail — and revelations that Mangione’s private writings lambasted health insurers as greedy, according to authorities — made the case a fulcrum for debate about the industry and made Mangione a cause célèbre for some of its critics.
Mangione told the court Friday that he pursued Thompson “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”
Mangione never was a UnitedHealthcare customer, according to police and the company. A University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, he was arrested five days after the shooting, when he was spotted at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pa. It’s about 230 miles west of Manhattan.
Thompson led one of the United States’ largest health insurers, but he wasn’t well known outside the industry. Trained as an accountant, he had worked at parent company UnitedHealth Group Inc. for 20 years and became CEO of its insurance arm, UnitedHealthcare, in 2021. He and his wife have two sons, who were in high school when their father was killed.
Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence for Mangione. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed him to a potential death penalty.
Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition.”
Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first.
The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.
In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.
Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defense, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.
They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and a notebook in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.
In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defense in the state case but reversed course a day later. The defense, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.
—Michael R. Sisak, Larry Neumeister, and Alanna Durkin Richer

A Bleak, Violent Novel’s Unexpected Delights
For the characters in The Disappearers, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death.
This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.
Before his latest book, Marlon James hadn’t written a novel set in Jamaica in more than a decade. In the years following his Booker Prize–winning A Brief History of Seven Killings, the author focused on his Dark Star Trilogy, set in a fantasy universe. But after that long literary detour, he returned to the land of his birth in his new novel, The Disappearers—which is set primarily in Kingston and follows a group of characters, all queer Jamaican men, who meet while rehearsing a play that will never be seen.
First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section:
For this group, which gathers in secret in 1988, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death. The Kingston they inhabit is murderously homophobic, and accordingly, the novel can be quite bleak. But The Disappearers offers some delights too. Recently, in her article about the book for The Atlantic, Stephanie Burt noted that “the novel opens up many pleasures for literary readers,” who may recognize the numerous titles and references sprinkled throughout. I was deeply affected by how, almost universally, the characters seek out anything that proves that gay life exists on a larger scale. Lowbrow works, such as porn films and magazines, are most accessible; Playgirl and Hustler are name-checked. The songs of Boy George, Sylvester, and Prince are lifelines—the homoerotic cover of Prince’s 1988 album, Lovesexy, is an especially powerful beacon. Many of the characters are well read, and they name-drop gay novels such as Andrew Holleran’s Dancer From the Dance and E. M. Forster’s Maurice. For one of the men in particular, the type of hustling, defiant gay life that John Rechy describes in his nonfiction book The Sexual Outlaw is pivotal.
The play they put on, a 1967 drama called Fortune and Men’s Eyes, explores homosexuality among a group of prisoners. Some of its characters see sex as a means for gaining or establishing power; others, as a convenient way to access pleasure. Some are what a modern audience might recognize as gay, whereas others choose partners largely because of their proximity. The cast share the characters’ disparate attitudes toward queerness. But in the Jamaica they live in, there is no room for nuance; any man seen as homosexual is a target for violence. Brutality will soon come to the rehearsal room.
In a way, James has written a gay novel about the uses of a gay novel. When his characters invoke Oscar Wilde and Edmund White, Hadrian and Michelangelo, they’re proving, to themselves and to the reader, that queer life existed long before they came around. But James is not an unskeptical cheerleader for the healing power of visibility and representation. The Disappearers’ major theme, after all, is that being recognized can be a bad thing: Owning these books is a hazard. Buying Lovesexy as a man in 1988 Kingston invites vigilantism. Staging Fortune and Men’s Eyes puts its cast and crew in danger.
So why try to do it? The director and ringleader, Havelock Titus, asks himself this question more than a decade after those hopeful rehearsals. He knew, even at the time, that the effort was a risk. He still doesn’t know “what success would have meant,” because the unstaged play “never had the chance to become a failure.” But Havelock knows on some level that he did it because, just like those who came before him, he wanted to create some kind of evidence that gay men communed and survived in his time and place. In short, he was tired of being erased.
Marlon James Returns to Realism, and to Jamaica
By Stephanie Burt
In his new novel, gay men struggle to escape violence in Kingston.
What to Read
The Age of Reform, by Richard Hofstadter
History can’t fully explain the present or predict the future, but it can help us understand the patterns of contemporary politics and the likely paths ahead. In 1955, Hofstadter, one of the great American historians of the 20th century, published The Age of Reform—a political and social history of the years 1890 to 1940, the period of populism, progressivism, and the New Deal. Rapid technological change, monopoly power, deep inequality, endemic corruption, mass immigration, nativist demagogues, the transformation of both political parties, repeated efforts at reform, recurring spasms of reaction: Perhaps no other age so resembles our own. Hofstadter is brilliant at analyzing types that feel quite familiar to us today—the crusading urban progressive, the small-town conspiracy theorist. He was a liberal who sympathized with the passion for progress while unsentimentally diagnosing its illiberal ideas and motives. The fevered moralism of that age seems a long way from the paralyzing cynicism of ours. But reading Hofstadter will remind you that reform and reaction not only follow each other, but also often coexist in the same moment; neither ever has the last word. Americans are always dreaming of a better country, and some have actually made it so. — George Packer

Four delicious and easy noodle dishes to mix up your weeknights
Noodles are budget-friendly, filling and fun — as well as incredibly versatile.
They also have an amazing ability to get fussy eaters (if you happen to have them in your household) enthusiastic about a variety of food.
You can pick the type of noodles you use, depending on dietary requirements or what you have available, for any of these recipes.
Sticky beef with noodles, pickled celery and mint
The perfect base for slow-cooked beef isn't a bun — it's noodles.
Beef chuck is a budget-friendly cut that slow-cooks brilliantly while you get on with your day. The sticky sauce in Ismat Awan's recipe coats the noodles and contrasts with the cool crunch of the pickled celery.
You can swap out chuck for blade, shin or brisket too.
Vegetable and soba noodle salad with honey ginger cashews
Loaded with veggies and a delicious mix of textures, Heidi Sze's soba noodle salad has a tasty dressing with Asian flavours and sweet crunchy cashews.
The veggies take a little bit of chopping time, but you can reduce this by buying them pre-chopped, prepping them ahead of time or with the careful use of a mandolin (you want to cut prep time, not your fingers).
One-pot udon noodles with kimchi and cheese
Spicy, cheesy and satisfying, this dish from Hetty Lui McKinnon takes the perfect pairing of kimchi and cheese to another level by combining it with chubby udon noodles and a thick, gravy-like sauce.
It's a delicious way to use kimchi — even if you're not yet a convert — and you can mix up the cheese you use.
Green ginger and miso noodles
This little gem of a meal from Phoebe Thorburn takes just 20 minutes to have ready and is gluten-free, dairy-free and plant-based (but doesn't have to be if that's not what you need).
Sauteed garlic, ginger and miso are blended with spinach, and a few other easy and tasty additions, to make a vibrant sauce that coats the noodles.
Adding spring onion and crispy chilli to serve gives it a perfect kick and crunch.

Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.
The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.
Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.
By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:
 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons
  564,970 parts of explosive ordnance
  298 components of military vehicles
Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.)
An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.
Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.
Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.
The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.
Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”
The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.
The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.
“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.
Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.
India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.

Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president?
- Published
For now, beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino still has some allies in world football, particularly in parts of the world where less well-off football associations have benefited from his presidency.
Infantino's position has been under scrutiny since his controversial plan to sell stakes in Fifa's global competitions to private investors was scrapped having been opposed by some regional governing bodies.
Late on Thursday, the executive committee of the African confederation (Caf) unanimously confirmed its support for Infantino, after leading African football administrators sent messages backing him.
Five of the seven African countries on the Fifa Council - Egypt, Morocco, Niger, Mauritania and Comoros - have already supported him publicly.
Support from the continent largely stems from Fifa's Forward programme, a funding scheme Infantino introduced in 2016 that many African federations have become increasingly reliant on to fund football projects in areas where commercial and government investment in the sport is limited.
Our reporters and correspondents have explained below where some of Africa's key footballing nations stand.
Morocco
Morocco's rise as one of Africa's football success stories has largely been driven by government funding, but the country has also become a key partner for Fifa.
Morocco's capital, Rabat, is home to Fifa's Africa regional office, they have hosted Fifa Club World Cups, a women's U17 World Cup and will co-host the men's 2030 World Cup alongside Spain and Portugal.
Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) president Fouzi Lekjaa reaffirmed his support for Infantino after he withdrew the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal last week.
In a statement, Lekjaa described Infantino's decision to withdraw it as "wise", adding it put the unity of Fifa's 211 member associations first.
Infantino also received the backing of senior football executives at a meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, following a turbulent period after the proposal's collapse.
Reporting by Celestine Karoney
Egypt
Egypt is home to the Confederation of African Football headquarters and remains one of Infantino's strongest institutional allies in Africa.
The relationship is reinforced by the influence of Hany Abo Rida, a Fifa Council member and one of the continent's most prominent football administrators, who has maintained close ties with Infantino since his election in 2016.
During Infantino's presidency, Egypt has benefited from Fifa's Forward programme, which has funded infrastructure projects, youth development, coach education and women's football.
Like other African member associations, the Egyptian Football Association has also received increased development funding under Fifa's expanded investment strategy, while new and expanded football competitions have created additional commercial and sporting opportunities.
But support for Infantino in Egypt is accompanied by growing expectations. Officials and observers increasingly argue that Fifa's engagement with Africa should extend beyond financial assistance. Greater emphasis is being placed on good governance, transparency, sustainable football development and giving Cafmore room to shape the continent's own priorities.
Reporting by Mohamed Alkaaoud in Cairo
DR Congo
The Congolese Football Federation (Fecofa) has welcomed Infantino's decision to withdraw the controversial Forward Enterprise proposal, calling it "wise" in a statement earlier this month.
Pointing to a decade of work promoting football worldwide - and in particular his support of African nations - the federation stressed that the episode should not overshadow Infantino's wider record.
Fecofa stressed that the episode, born of good intentions, should not overshadow Infantino's wider record. It pointed to his decade of work promoting football worldwide, and particularly his support for African federations and those with fewer resources.
The federation said it had "greatly benefited" from Fifa's programmes, citing investment in development and infrastructure.
The declaration was signed by Véron Mosengo‑Omba, elected president of Fecofa in May 2026. His election ended a period of uncertainty following the resignation of Constant Omari Selemani in 2021 and the subsequent Fifa‑appointed Normalisation Committee established in April 2023.
Mosengo‑Omba assured Infantino of Fecofa's "full support" would continue beyond 2027, recalling mandates renewed in Paris in 2019 and Kigali in 2023. The statement underlines the Democratic Republic of Congo's alignment with Fifa leadership at a time when divisions remain sharp elsewhere in world football.
Reporting by Emery Makumeno
Nigeria
The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has largely aligned itself towards a supportive stance for Infantino's leadership, despite the wider backlash globally.
For a football federation facing chronic funding constraints and enormous infrastructure needs, Infantino's proposed plans would have been difficult to dismiss.
Former president of the NFF and deputy chairman of Fifa's Men's National Teams Competitions Committee, Amaju Pinnick, argued that Infantino's plan would deliver a much-needed financial boost to every member association without over-relying on local governments.
Nigeria is eligible for up to $8m (£5.95m), for the current Fifa Forward funding, despite failing to qualify for the last two men's World Cup tournaments.
The most prominent Forward project currently under way in Nigeria is the redevelopment of the NFF Technical Centre in the capital, Abuja. The project, funded with approximately $4.88m, includes the reconstruction of training pitches, and the construction of a modern accommodation complex for Nigeria's national teams.
Reporting by Emmanuel Akindubuwa
What others in Africa have said
The Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture of South Africa, Gayton McKenzie, posted on X saying that Infantino had been "very good to African football".
"Africa should be cautious in joining the public lynching of Infantino. He has been very good to African football.
"We can debate his ideas but let's not forget who has been a friend to us. Many of those calling for his head want the old status quo back too."
Speaking to the BBC after Infantino's proposal emerged, football officials from Malawi and Uganda said Fifa investment had transformed the game both on and off the pitch, arguing such funding is vital given the financial realities facing many African nations.
"Malawi needs money. Malawi needs stadiums, our government cannot manage to give us even $1m every year for football," Malawi FA president Fleetwood Haiya told BBC's Newsday programme.
"Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals [and] at the same time to look at football," he said.
President of the Gambia Football Federation, Lamin Kaba Bajo, told BBC Sport: "As far as I'm concerned, most of my colleagues are concerned, we'll encourage him [Infantino] to stay, and we'll do everything within our means to ensure that he is re-elected come next year, 2027.
"That's my personal opinion as president of the federation, and a good number of African memberships also stand on that line. He is here to stay."
But support for the project on the continent was not universal. Former Sierra Leone FA president and ex-Fifa Council member Isha Johansen was among African voices opposing it, warning it risked over-commercialising football asking, "What price does one have to pay in order to get to this elevated development for football in Africa?"
Johansen urged African football chiefs to think carefully about the game's future.
Last month, Caf president Patrice Motsepe lauded Infantino for his "excellent work" after this year's World Cup and hailed him as "a good friend".
"He is loyal to Africa," Motsepe said on 22 July. "When people have been loyal to you, you never stab them in the back."
Other nations are yet to comment publicly, including Senegal, whose men's team is the second-highest ranked African team behind Morocco.

‘Dimagi Naxal Party’ springs up on Instagram after PM Modi’s remark, over 1 lakh people follow in 24 hours
According to the ‘Dimagi Naxal Party’ introduction on Instagram and X, its motto is “Think | Research | Resist.”
A day after Prime Minister Narendra Modi used the term “dimagi Naxals”, a satirical party based on the term has emerged, garnering support from people online.
An Instagram account called “Dimagi Naxal Party” has surfaced and gained over 1,81,000 followers overnight. The party also has an X account named “Dimagi Naxal Janta Party” with over 7 thousand followers.
According to the party’s bios on Instagram and X, its motto is “Think | Research | Resist.” The Instagram bio says the founder of the party is “A Dimagi Indian,” while the co-founder is someone with “56 Inch ka.”
While the exact date the Instagram account was created is not known, the party’s X account was created in August 2026.
The party on Monday also alleged that its Instagram account had come under cyberattacks. “Cyber Attack Started against @DNJP_India on Instagram. Let’s see if they succeed to curb our voices!” it wrote on X.
What is the party's ideology?
According to posts on the party’s Instagram and X accounts, it says it is following the ideology of Bhagat Singh.
In one post, the party wrote: “We are Followers of Bhagat Singh… If THEY try to suspend our accounts or label us Anti-Nationals, just know — they are disrespecting Bhagat Singh.”
What led to DNP?
The move comes after PM Modi in his Independence Day address to the nation warned against what he described as “dimagi Naxals” (intellectual Naxals), saying that while the government had won against armed Maoists, people sympathetic to the ideology were still looking for opportunities to influence and “brainwash” the youth. He called for identifying and isolating such ‘dimaagi Naxal.”
“LWE extremism destroyed the future of lakhs of youths. Naxal violence and ideology snatched the children of so many mothers. This Naxal violence, for many decades, had controlled a large part of the country and ruled by the gun,” he said on Saturday.
His comments drew sharp criticism from Opposition parties with Congress labelling the new terminology a “sure sign of desperation.”
“First he called his opponents ‘urban naxals’. Now he calls them ‘dimaagi Naxals’. It is a sure sign of his desperation,” Ramesh posted on X, adding that the prime minister frequently ends up adopting policies advocated by those he criticises. “It is not for nothing that the PM has an MA being the ‘Master Abuser’ in Entire Political Science that he is.”
Senior Congress leader P Chidambaram remarked, "I am proud to be a dimagi naxal".
Cockroach Janta Party's Saurav Das also hit back at the prime minister, rejecting his classification of critical youth. Taking to X, he said, “Dimagi Naxal or whatever is not going to work, Prime Minister. How could you loosely brand educated young people ‘Naxalis’ etc.? Just because they question your government? Sheer arrogance! Sheer incompetence at resolving their problems?”
Following criticism from the Opposition, Union minister of parliamentary affairs Kiren Rijiju hit out at opposition parties, insisting that the PM did not refer to opposition leaders as ‘dimagi naxal', or people with a Naxal mindset.
"PM @narendramodi ji didn't say opposition leaders as Dimagi Naxals. Only following are Dimagi Naxals: 1. Who support Maoists and reject Indian Constitution. 2. Who stand with separatists & support Article 370. 4. Who want to cut chicken neck to separate North-East from India," Rijiju wrote on X.

Teen jailed for exam cheating in Guinea dies after sickle cell complications, father says
- Published
The father of a teenager from Guinea with sickle cell disease who died days after he was arrested for cheating in an exam has told the BBC he blames the authorities for his death.
Mamadou Djouma Bah, 17, was transferred to hospital after his health deteriorated while in prison and later died "under the care of his treating physician", according to the prosecutor.
His father, Mamadou Saliou Bah, has called for an investigation, telling the BBC that his son did not "receive good medical care" in detention.
People with sickle cell are often at an increased risk of contracting serious infections or they can become anaemic, which is when red blood cells cannot carry enough oxygen around the body.
- What is sickle cell disease? 
  - Published19 June 2023
Sickle cell disease is a lifelong illness, common in people of African descent, and caused by a faulty gene that produces unusually shaped red blood cells that can become stuck in blood vessels.
This can lead to severely painful episodes, which experts say can sometimes be prevented by wrapping up warm and drinking plenty of fluid, and daily antibiotics can reduce risk of infections. Other treatments can include blood transfusions.
The sudden pain in the chest, limbs, back and joints - from a lack of blood circulation - may cause organ damage.
'Dad, I'm dying'
Djouma Bah - who was a social sciences student - had allegedly been caught using his phone during Guinea's national school-leaving baccalaureate on 15 July, when he was arrested with other students, also suspected of exam fraud.
Two days later, he was convicted for cheating and sentenced to six months in prison, five of which were suspended.
He was serving his one month in a prison in the city of Kindia, about 137km (85 miles) north-east of the capital, Conakry, when his health deteriorated.
The teenager was subsequently transferred to the regional hospital for treatment.
Saliou Bah told the BBC that when he visited his son in hospital, the boy said he could not breathe properly and asked to lean against him.
"Then he looked at me and said: 'Dad, I'm dying,'" Saliou Bah said.
"Those were his last words."
The teenager spent around two days in hospital before being discharged to go home, where he died, according to officials.
Education Minister Alpha Bacar Barry said he was "deeply saddened by the news" and extended his "sincere condolences" to the family.
Human rights organisations are also calling for an independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death and the prosecution of other students.
On Wednesday, students demonstrated over the detentions of their fellow classmates, calling for their release.
"A student should not be sent to prison. These young people are the future of our country," Saliou Bah said.
"I also ask the authorities to release the other students who are still detained before they too lose their lives.
"We lost our son; we lost our future."

The first flight of the largest battery-electric aircraft to take to the skies lasted nearly half an hour while costing just $5 of electricity. That aviation feat comes at a time when jet fuel prices have skyrocketed because of the US war with Iran.
The test flight of Heart Aerospace’s X1 demonstrator aircraft took place at Plattsburgh International Airport in upstate New York on August 12. The X1 aircraft is comparable in size to a small regional airliner and can achieve a maximum takeoff weight exceeding 25,000 pounds with the help of four wing-mounted electric motors. The battery-electric propulsion system delivered more than one megawatt of power during the maiden flight.
All-electric aircraft can offer quieter and cleaner flight without the emissions that come from burning jet fuel. They may also prove more reliably cost-effective than conventional aircraft that come with jet fuel costs subject to geopolitical disruptions.
But the initial success of the X1 demonstrator does not mean Heart Aerospace is planning to commercialize an all-electric aircraft. Current battery-electric systems can only typically sustain short flights of about 100 to 200 miles, which is why they have been limited to air taxi operations by companies such as Joby and Archer.
Instead, testing of the X1 and a planned follow-on X2 aircraft will shape development of Heart Aerospace’s main offering to the airline industry—a 30-seat hybrid-electric regional airliner known as the ES-30.
That planned production aircraft for commercial flights would combine two inboard electric motors with commercial turboprop engines that run on jet fuel, enabling 125 miles of all-electric flight and 500 miles of flight range when operating in hybrid mode.
Looking to innovation as jet fuel prices rise
Having the extended 500-mile range would enable the ES-30 hybrid-electric airliner to operate in popular short-haul corridors that connect major US and European cities. United Airlines has committed to eventually purchasing 100 aircraft from Heart Aerospace, with other major airline customers also having signed letters of intent, according to Flying magazine.

Ukraine launches one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, killing at least 6 people in Russia
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones across Russia Sunday, killing at least six people in one of Kyiv's largest aerial attacks of the war.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said that it had destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones overnight. Some 600 drones were detected headed toward the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, with a third destroyed over the Moscow region itself.
An 83-year-old man was killed after a Ukrainian drone hit a private home in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said. He also confirmed that a Ukrainian attack had sparked a blaze at a warehouse belonging to Russian retail giant Wildberries in the town of Podolsk, where images shared by Russian media outlets showed columns of black smoke .
A drone attack targeted three towns in Russia's southwestern Rostov region, killing five people, local Gov. Yury Slyusar said. The attack, with more than 150 drones, damaged several homes and a railway station and sparked a forest fire.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Russia this year, with long-range missiles and swarms of drones increasingly targeting military industries and energy facilities. It has also increasingly pummeled giant Wildberries depots, burning billions of dollars' worth of merchandise and bringing the war home to the Russian public nearly 4½ years into Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russian strike kills 3 in Ukraine
A Russian missile attack on Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 14 others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media Sunday. He also said that one more person had been killed in the city of Sumy.
Meanwhile, a Russian attack on Kyiv sparked fires throughout the Ukrainian capital and injured six people.
"Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure," Zelenskyy said. "Since this morning, air raid alerts have continued in many regions – the Russians launched another wave of drones."

Movie that went viral for terrible animation becomes China box office hit
- Published
It's so bad, it's become a box office hit.
Niu Lai, a low-budget animation film about a cow in a dream sequence has seen a huge jump in ticket sales after going viral for its confusing plot and terrible graphics.
It grossed just 7,705 yuan ($1,140; £843) in the first 10 days after its release, but has now made more than 11.4 million yuan, according to movie tracking site Mao Yan. That means it is holding ground against Hollywood blockbusters like The Odyssey and Spider Man: Brand New Day.
"You may regret for 80 minutes if you watch it, but if you don't, you'll regret it for life," one popular social media post about the film said.
Other social media users have hailed the movie as the antidote to the AI slop that is taking over social media algorithms.
They are sharing clips praising Niu Lai's "hand-crafted" method - a reference to the poor animation quality - as "proof" that its creators did not use AI.
"That's some serious craftsmanship," a Weibo user wrote.
Another social media user called it "pure handmade" and the biggest "dark horse" of the summer movie season.
Others say they are rooting for the movie because they desperately hope for a "bullish" stock market.
"If the index reaches 4,000 tomorrow I will go to the cinema to support this movie," one Weibo user wrote.
"It is a terrible movie but has a great name," another comment linking the movie to stock investments said.
Niu Lai was a low-budget, lowkey production from the outset, and had received almost no publicity before its release earlier this month.
But now it has proved so popular that cinemas have added screenings of the film in response to the soaring demand.
"This record is unprecedented and will likely remain so," a Weibo account dedicated to tracking movies noted.
But not everyone is celebrating its unexpected success. Over the weekend, a commentary by state-owned Beijing News warned that cinemas risk "losing the trust" of viewers if they "continue to lower their standard" with additional screenings of Niu Lai.
Mentioning previous movies that had been mocked for poor quality, Niu Lai has "once again lowered the bar for audiences' expectations of poorly made films", reads a commentary by state-owned Beijing News.
It urged cinemas to "act as gatekeepers for the audience, and clearly reject films that are obviously not up to standard instead of letting films like Niu Lai run rampant".

New Delhi, Aug 17: President Droupadi Murmu has given assent to a bill to rename Kerala as Keralam, with the legislation now becoming a law.
The Lok Sabha passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026, on Tuesday, followed by the Rajya Sabha the next day.
In the Rajya Sabha, Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai said the Kerala Assembly passed a resolution in 2024, urging the Centre to bring a law to change the name of the state to Keralam.
"The bill provides that the State of Kerala will be known as the State of Keralam, and hence there is a proposal to rename the State of Kerala to Keralam," he said.
The Kerala government had forwarded a resolution passed by the state assembly regarding the name change to the Centre in June 2024.
Subsequently, President Murmu referred the Bill to the state legislature for its views, following which the Assembly adopted a unanimous resolution agreeing with the Bill.
The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill provides for the alteration of the state's name and contains necessary amendments to the Constitution and consequential provisions, according to the Bill's statement of objects and reasons.
Amendments will be made in the First Schedule to the Constitution by modifying the name of Kerala as Keralam in accordance with Article 3 of the Constitution.

A new survey in Arunachal Pradesh has documented recurring experiences of widespread harassment of members of the LGBTQIA+ community in the State.
Also read | On India’s rainbow trail | Queer-focused walks are finding an audience in the country
According to the Itanagar-based HimKai Research Institute (HRI), the pestering or provocation has led to identity concealment, discrimination-related distress, and low confidence in institutional protection among the LGBTQIA+ respondents in the State.
LGBTQIA+ expands to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer or Questioning, Intersex, and Asexual.
The HRI conducted the anonymous online survey between June 2 and August 2. It received 62 submissions, one of which was excluded during geographic eligibility and data-quality screening because the self-reported home district could not be mapped in Arunachal Pradesh.
“Among the 61 respondents included in the analysis, 49.2% said they hid their gender identity or sexual orientation most of the time or always because of fear of discrimination or violence. Half of valid respondents said they felt accepted within their family rarely or never, while 44.3% said they felt safe in their local community rarely or never,” the HRI report said.
“Experiences of harassment and discrimination were reported across several settings. Some 91.8% of respondents reported verbal harassment at least rarely, while 52.5% reported physical threats or violence at least rarely. Among valid responses, 85.0% reported discrimination in school or college at least rarely, and 63.2% reported workplace discrimination,” it said.
The survey also found that 72.9% of valid respondents felt compelled to change their behaviour or appearance sometimes or more often to retain work or education. A further 57.9% said their identity affected access to employment or income opportunities at least rarely.
Religious, cultural exclusion
“Mental wellbeing emerged as a significant concern. Among valid responses, 76.7% reported experiencing stress, anxiety or emotional distress related to discrimination sometimes or more often, including 48.3% who experienced it most of the time or always. Access to mental-health or peer support was uneven: 41.0% said such support was available most of the time or always, while 36.1% said it was available rarely or never,” the report said.
The findings also point to a gap between awareness of rights and confidence in institutions. While 56.7% of valid respondents agreed that they were aware of their legal rights, 63.3% disagreed that laws and policies adequately protect LGBTQIA+ persons, and 66.7% disagreed that police and authorities respond sensitively to LGBTQIA+ issues.
Religion, culture and social belonging received particularly cautious assessments. Some 72.1% did not agree that religion or faith practices are accepting of LGBTQIA+ persons. More than half disagreed that their identity is compatible with their cultural or tribal background or that local traditions allow space for diverse identities, with 51.7% of valid respondents disagreeing that they feel a sense of belonging in society.
Healthcare emerged as a comparatively more positive area. Among valid respondents, 56.7% said that they felt comfortable accessing healthcare most of the time or always, and 75.0% said healthcare providers treated them with respect most of the time or always.
“Friends were the most frequently reported source of support, mentioned by 37 respondents, followed by LGBTQIA+ networks, mentioned by 12.
Six respondents mentioned. Awareness and sensitisation were the most common single priority identified for improving LGBTQIA+ lives in Arunachal Pradesh, followed by legal protection,” the report said.
HRI director Ranju Dodum said the study was intended to begin building locally grounded evidence on experiences that are often discussed without adequate data.
“LGBTQIA+ experiences in Arunachal Pradesh cannot simply be assumed from national conversations. Family, community, tribal identity, religion, education and employment all shape how people experience acceptance and safety here. This is a baseline study and its numbers must be read with methodological caution, but they point to questions that deserve deeper research and serious public discussion,” he said.
The report recommends sustained sensitisation programmes in schools, colleges, workplaces, healthcare institutions, police and public administration; confidential mechanisms for reporting discrimination; stronger mental-health and peer-support systems; safe community spaces; more inclusive education and workplace practices; and locally grounded engagement with families, community institutions and faith leaders.
The survey sample was predominantly young, with 90.2% of respondents between 18 and 35 years.

Jason Arday, Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism, is found dead
LONDON — A British sociologist who resigned last week from the University of Cambridge following weeks of public accusations of plagiarism and media scrutiny was found dead Friday.
Jason Arday, who was 37 when he became Cambridge's youngest Black professor in 2023, resigned after he came under intense media pressure, with weeks of allegations about plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.
The Times and Telegraph newspapers, along with the BBC and Sky News, reported that Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" inside a home in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.
News of his death comes the same week as the release of his memoir, "Great and Unfortunate Things," a highly anticipated work that Simon & Schuster had decided to release despite the doubts about his credibility. In a statement issued through his publisher, Arday's family said that they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," the family said, adding that for three years Arday was "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse ... by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him."
The Metropolitan Police said only that a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead in Battersea, without naming the man, in accordance with its policy.
"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," the police statement said.
Cambridge Vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university will investigate the circumstances around Arday's employment, said she was "desperately saddened" by the news.
"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.
In resigning as professor of sociology of education, Arday wrote in a statement that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
He said his stepping down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." He has denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate.
Supporters, including more than two dozen academics and politicians, had described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."
Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.
Cambridge has opened investigation into plagiarism accusations
In his memoir, Arday wrote of himself as born to achieve and born to struggle. He remembered a family "legend" that the 1980s hit "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" was on the radio at the time of his birth. He described how a midwife noted his long fingers and told his mother that it was a sign he was meant for greatness. In his early 20s, he recalled, he was on a relief mission in Brazil when an aid worker placed a hand on his arm and also predicted an extraordinary life.
"But I also believe you're destined for very sad and difficult things as well," she warned him.
Questions about Arday's qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a one-time Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his critique of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.
On July 24, the Times of London published an analysis of Arday's 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.
British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($7.4 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.
Dozens of Cambridge academics had signed a letter calling for an independent inquiry into how Arday was appointed. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.
The university then changed its stance and said it opened an investigation "following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."
Prentice, the university's vice-chancellor, said this week that Cambridge will run a review of its hiring processes. She stressed that "our staff of color are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community."
"This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge," she said Thursday.

Why Trump is tearing up a beloved national park
Big Bend National Park is the latest casualty of Trump’s border wall obsession.
Welcome to The Logoff: Remember President Donald Trump’s first-term border wall? It’s still being built — through a pristine Texas national park.
What’s happening? The Trump administration is preparing to build hundreds of miles of roads through Big Bend National Park in southwest Texas as part of its latest border security project, despite a bipartisan outcry over damage to the beloved park.
Starting last week, bulldozers and heavy machinery began to clear land for the construction of about 200 miles of patrol road, new border barriers, and electronic surveillance measures to cover the park’s 118 miles of shared border with Mexico. The construction is proceeding after the administration overrode environmental laws intended to protect places like Big Bend earlier this year.
What does a border wall look like in 2026? In this case, “wall” is a bit of a misnomer. Despite Trump’s fixation with an actual, physical wall circa 2016, the Trump administration’s current project isn’t always 30 feet high and topped with concertina wire.
Instead, the Big Bend project is part of what the administration has described as a “smart wall,” which will combine stretches of traditional wall elsewhere along the US-Mexico border with patrol roads and vehicle barriers like those planned for the park, all blanketed with surveillance.
It’s a small retreat from the administration’s original plan for a border wall through Big Bend, which sparked outrage earlier this year. Still, the administration intends to build about 700 additional miles of “primary” wall, spanning all four border states. The whole project is slated to cost around $47 billion.
Why Big Bend? It’s hard to say. As the New York Times reported earlier this year, the park has long been considered low-priority given its remote location and inhospitable weather. Only about 1 percent of those apprehended for crossing the US-Mexico border have been detained in Big Bend.

As rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administered Kashmir. His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier.
“I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, a cloudburst sent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside.
Latief, 48, had spent years building the house, where five generations of his Gujjar family lived together. Within minutes, the torrent swallowed it, trapping eight family members inside. He survived only because he had stepped outside. By dawn, everything he had built lay in rubble.
When the Guardian reached Murrah four days later, electricity, roads and mobile networks were cut off. Floodwaters had washed away roads and footbridges, leaving the only way into the village a 90-minute walk through rain and landslide debris. Residents carried sacks of flour, cooking gas cylinders and medicines across the broken crossing.
Murrah is perched high in the Pir Panjal range above the town of Bafliaz, in Poonch district, about 125 miles (200km) south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir’s main city. The village is home to mostly Gujjars, one of the largest pastoralist communities in the Himalayas, whose livelihoods have long depended on livestock, farming and seasonal migration through the mountains.
The hillside remained too unstable for excavators to reach. Soldiers, disaster response teams and local volunteers searched the debris by hand while others combed the swollen Suran River for the missing.
Latief now lives in the house of his brother, Mohd Bashir, just above the landslide. Inside, women gathered to mourn while men quietly received visitors offering condolences. Verses from the Qur’an echoed through the house.
“I built that house for my family,” Latief said, holding up pictures of his 16-year-old son Sajjad Ahmed, an aspiring cricketer, whose body was still missing. Days before the disaster, the family recorded videos together.
As mourners gathered, news spread that another body had been found several miles down the river; the room fell silent as another funeral procession passed through the village.
Among those searching was Mohammad Razak, 45, who had spent four days combing the river with a team of volunteers. “We’ve been searching every bend of the river,” he said. “We’re still hoping we’ll find them.”
Murrah was among the worst-hit places after a series of cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides swept Jammu and Kashmir this month, killing at least 28 people. Scientists say rising temperatures are increasing the likelihood of short, intense rainfall events across the western Himalayas. In steep mountainous terrain, these rains can trigger rapid flooding and landslides, putting remote communities at increased risk. For mountain communities, the climate crisis is also exacerbating longstanding geographical and social vulnerabilities.
The destruction stretched far beyond Murrah. About 30 miles away in Rajouri, the Manawar Tawi River burst its banks, washing away roads, dozens of vehicles and the town’s main Bela bus station.
Low-lying settlements along the riverbank were submerged in mud and debris. Several houses collapsed across the Pir Panjal mountains, livestock were swept away and hundreds of families were displaced.
About 180 miles north, in Gurez Valley near the line of control with Pakistan-administered Kashmir, residents say they are seeing the same pattern. A cloudburst in Achoora village on 20 July damaged the crops of 11 families and blocked the valley’s only road.
Residents say increasingly erratic rainfall is disrupting farming and making traditional livelihoods more precarious. It followed a series of cloudbursts that hit Gurez and neighbouring Tulail over the past month, damaging homes, farmland, bridges, and roads.
“People knew when the snow would come and when to plant crops,” said Aamir Asghar Khan, 26, a resident of Achoora. “Nothing seems predictable any more. The rain is getting more intense every year, and the frequent cloudbursts are threatening our livelihoods.”
Heavy rainfall also triggered devastating floods and landslides in Ladakh and across the border in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, reinforcing concerns that increasingly erratic weather is affecting communities across the western Himalayas.
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (Icimod) said the western Himalayas were experiencing frequent bursts of intense rainfall capable of triggering floods, landslides and cloudbursts. Accelerating glacier melt is likely to increase flood risks in the short term before reducing water availability in coming decades.
“The challenge our mountain communities face is twofold – too much water at times and too little at others,” an expert from Icimod said. “Adaptation requires work on both fronts, managing flood risk and water scarcity together.”
ICIMOD said priorities included expanding community-based early warning systems, installing more weather stations in high-altitude areas, restoring damaged watersheds and designing roads and other infrastructure for future weather conditions rather than historical weather patterns.
Dr Suheel Rasool Mir, a Kashmir-based sociologist who studies Indigenous communities in Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, said pastoral communities were among the first to bear the consequences of erratic weather as their livelihoods relied directly on forests, rivers, grazing lands and seasonal migration.
“For Gujjar, Bakarwal and Dard-Shin communities, these disasters are not simply natural hazards,” he said. “As climate extremes become more frequent, they lose not only homes and livestock but also the ecological knowledge and ancestral livelihoods that have sustained them for generations.”
For Latief back in Murrah, only one hope remained. “I just want to find them,” he said. “Then we can bury our family together.”

If you’ve followed mental health topics on TikTok or Instagram lately, you have probably heard the term emotional regulation. But emotional regulation isn’t just a trendy buzzword. It’s a nuanced concept that psychologists like me have been studying for decades.
At its core, emotional regulation is how well someone can manage their emotions – whether positive ones like excitement and joy, or negative or more uncomfortable ones like jealousy and anger.
I study emotional regulation – which scientists refer to as simply “emotion regulation” – within the context of relationships, including understanding how children learn to regulate their own emotions. The goal of healthy emotional regulation is not to erase difficult feelings, but to be able to manage those feeling more effectively so they do not become overwhelming.
Emotional regulation versus temperament
People often confuse emotional regulation with temperament, which is your natural, inborn style for how you approach or react to the world. Psychologists describe three different types of temperament that a person can have: easy and flexible; active, outgoing and excitable; or cautious and quiet. Temperament is genetically and biologically driven – in other words, it is something you are born with.
Emotional regulation, on the other hand, isn’t something people either have or don’t have. It is a set of skills that develops over time, beginning in childhood as children learn from and interact with the people around them. And like other skills, emotional regulation can be strengthened with instruction and practice.
There are two types of emotional regulation: self-regulation, or managing your own emotions, and co-regulation, which involves helping others manage their emotions. Both are important in romantic relationships, at work and in parenting.
Co-regulation is especially important as a way to help kids respond to intense feelings.
Taming emotional cycles
Emotions don’t exist on their own. They are part of an ongoing conversation between your mind, your body and your behavior. The way you think affects how your body responds, your body’s reactions influence how you feel, and your feelings shape what you do.
For example, imagine someone cuts you off in traffic. Within moments, several things happen at once. You may feel a surge of rage as your heart starts racing, your palms begin to sweat, and thoughts like “What a #$% jerk!” flash through your mind. Those reactions may lead you to respond by rolling your eyes, swearing at the steering wheel or flipping off the driver.
Each of these reactions influences the others, creating an emotional cycle that can escalate or de-escalate, depending on how you respond. Understanding this cycle is important because changing just one part of it can shift the entire emotional experience.
Responding instead of reacting
Everyone engages in emotional regulation throughout the day – whether consciously or not. Healthy emotional regulation allows people to use their emotions as valuable sources of information rather than letting them take over their lives or ruin their day.
Emotions can signal that something feels threatening, unfair, exciting, disappointing or important, prompting you to pause and consider what might have triggered the reaction.
In the traffic example above, anger may be a clue that you perceived the other driver’s behavior as dangerous or disrespectful. Your emotion doesn’t mean your interpretation is wrong or right, but it does provide useful information about how you are experiencing the situation, which can help you decide how to respond.
Many people use emotional regulation strategies intentionally during the day to deal with uncomfortable or intense emotions. These include taking a walk, venting to a friend or shooting hoops. Or they might include less healthy options, such as doomscrolling, being irritable with loved ones or pouring that third glass of wine.
Multiple factors, such as life stressors – even sleep quality – can make it harder for people to regulate or contain tough emotions, increasing the risk of less-than-healthy coping strategies.
When emotional regulation falls short
We psychologists can’t talk about emotional regulation without talking about its opposite state – emotional dysregulation. That’s when you are not able to successfully use coping skills to deal with tough feelings, and those feelings then interfere with your ability to function.
Instead of using strategies that might serve as life rafts for when the seas of daily life become difficult, the waves wash over you – which can feel like you are drowning in the intensity of these feelings.
Yet it isn’t the emotion itself that’s the problem. Rather, it’s how you interpret the emotion, the story you tell yourself about it, and how you respond to it. When emotions become difficult to manage and begin interfering with how you think, act or function, that’s emotion dysregulation.
Prolonged emotion dysregulation has profound costs that extend far beyond how you feel in the moment.
Emotional dysregulation can affect a person’s physical health, including heart and immune system functioning, disrupt sleep, contribute to mental health problems and make it more difficult to be present and responsive in your relationships. It can also impair your memory, concentration and performance in everyday activities – not to mention your finances.
Research suggests that learning to address emotional dysregulation early on can reduce the risk of long-term consequences, including serious mental health conditions such as major mood disorders and borderline personality disorder.
Emotional regulation can be learned
Learning emotional regulation strategies begins with identifying your feelings and building a vocabulary to describe them. You can’t regulate what you can’t name.
Children learn emotional regulation skills by watching people around them. Parents and other caregivers can help their children by serving as an “emotional container,” naming emotions and modeling how to express them in a healthy way.
In the moment, emotional regulation strategies can include breathing or mindfulness techniques that help calm the body’s nervous system and turn down the intensity of emotions.
Longer term, skills from cognitive-behavioral therapy, one of the most effective forms of talk therapy for anxiety and depression, can help. These skills include learning to view difficult experiences as opportunities for growth, questioning unhelpful thoughts instead of automatically believing them, and accepting emotions without letting them take over.
Rather than trying to avoid or eliminate difficult feelings, the goal is to notice them and recognize that your emotions are not always accurate reflections of reality – in other words, that feelings are not facts. Then you can choose how to respond.
Talking through difficult emotions with someone you trust can help you feel understood, gain perspective and make it easier to respond thoughtfully rather than react impulsively.
Taking care of your body also supports emotional regulation. Getting enough sleep, eating a balanced diet and moving your body regularly helps your brain function at its best, making it easier to manage stress, think clearly and respond thoughtfully.
For healthy long-term emotional regulation skills, practicing matters. Just like working out your biceps in the gym, if you use these skills consistently, your capacity for responding can grow.
Jessica Griffin, Associate Professor of Psychiatry and Peditrics, UMass Chan Medical School
