A fabricated quote attributed to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards commander spread from an Indian X account to Israeli media and US politicians, eventually featuring in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech, according to a review by The New York Times.
The false claim emerged on August 5, when an anonymous account on X in India posted that Brig. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi had said Iran would not abandon its nuclear weapons ambitions as long as Israel and the United States possessed such weapons.
There is no evidence that Vahidi made the statement, or that Iran has developed nuclear weapons. Yet the claim quickly gained traction, with Israeli accounts and media outlets repeating it before it reached senior political figures in Israel and the United States.
The episode, detailed by The New York Times, shows how an unverified social media post can acquire credibility as it is repeatedly cited by politicians, broadcasters and other accounts, even when its original source is unreliable.
False quote gains traction in Israel
The fabricated quotation was first known to have appeared on an Indian X account with around 175,000 followers. The account has previously faced criticism from fact-checkers and Pakistan's government for allegedly spreading false and Islamophobic content, according to The New York Times.
The post included a photograph of Vahidi alongside a cartoonish, AI-generated mushroom cloud. The English text also contained spelling and grammatical errors.
Around two hours later, another Indian account with about 82,000 followers shared the same claim in Hindi. According to the Israeli fact-checking organisation Bodkim Project, that account had published another fabricated quote attributed to Vahidi a week earlier.
The narrative gained wider attention after it was shared by Mossad Commentary, a prominent Israeli X account that has no known connection to Israel's Mossad intelligence agency.
“The regime is not preparing to abandon its nuclear ambitions. It is buying time. There will be no deal,” the account posted.
The account is run by Gedaliah Blum, an entrepreneur who leads the Heartland Institute, which organises tours and promotional exchanges in Israel.
Blum told The New York Times that he believed the quotation came from a radio interview with Vahidi, although he could not remember the source. He said he shared it because he believed Iran was determined to acquire a nuclear weapon, despite uncertainty over “whether those exact words were spoken.”
About 30 minutes later, Israel's Channel 14 shared the quotation in English and claimed it represented the first public acknowledgement by Iran that it was pursuing a nuclear bomb. The post was viewed more than 440,000 times, according to The New York Times.
The claim then reached Yair Netanyahu, the son of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Within hours, it appeared in the prime minister's speech at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem.
“We heard today the commander of the I.R.G.C., Vahidi, explicitly declaring Iran’s intention to keep developing nuclear weapons,” Netanyahu said.
A spokesman for Netanyahu did not explain how the fabricated quotation came to be included in the speech, according to The New York Times, but defended the prime minister's longstanding warnings about Iran's nuclear programme.
On Azriel, a co-founder of the Bodkim fact-checking organisation, said the quotation “gained credibility every time an outlet or a politician repeated it,” helping drive its spread.
False claim reaches Washington
The claim soon crossed into the United States, where it was amplified by senior political figures and Fox News.
Mike Waltz, the Trump administration's ambassador to the United Nations, reposted the quotation and wrote that Iran was “finally admitting what’s been obvious for years”.
Republican Senator Rick Scott of Florida also shared the claim on social media.
Fox News host Bill Hemmer cited the purported statement during an interview with retired US Central Command commander Gen. Joseph L. Votel.
“That’s as close to an admission as I have heard, and we’ve been watching this story for years,” Hemmer said.
The narrative subsequently began to unravel. Waltz's post was removed from X, although no explanation was given. Neither Waltz nor the White House responded to requests for comment from The New York Times.
Fox News later acknowledged the problem. On Thursday, after inquiries from The New York Times, Hemmer read a statement on air saying Fox had learned that the quote was “unverified and inaccurate.”
Scott's post remained online, as did the original posts containing the fabricated quotation and thousands of responses treating it as genuine. Scott did not respond to a request for comment from The New York Times.
How the narrative gained credibility
Experts described the episode as an example of “narrative laundering”, in which an unverified or false claim is repeatedly passed between accounts and institutions until it appears to have multiple independent sources.
“This quote was clearly crafted to drive a wedge into peace negotiations,” said Darren L. Linvill of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, who tracks the spread of disinformation and propaganda on social media.
“It is a simple campaign,” he added, “but simple campaigns can still be very effective, and this seems to have certainly had bang for the buck.”
The sequence also illustrates how the apparent credibility of a claim can increase as it moves from social media accounts to television networks and political speeches, despite no new evidence being introduced.
The New York Times found it unclear who fabricated the quotation. However, the claim appeared to reinforce an existing narrative promoted by Netanyahu that Iran was determined to develop nuclear weapons and that military action against Tehran was necessary.
What Iran has said about its nuclear programme
Iran's nuclear programme has remained a major source of international concern and diplomatic negotiations for decades. Tehran has maintained that its nuclear activities have civilian purposes rather than a military objective, although the precise status of its nuclear development remains contested.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei criticised the fabricated claim and described it as “an example of the flood of lies against the Islamic republic.”
He blamed Israel for the narrative but did not provide evidence to support the allegation.
“The allegations of a link to a nuclear bomb are based on the same thing, a lie they have been feeding the international community for 20 years to justify military aggression,” he told reporters on Sunday.
Vahidi, who took command of the Revolutionary Guards in March, has issued numerous statements during the conflict but has not made the purported declaration about developing nuclear weapons.
Last year, after a 12-day conflict with Israel that ended with US airstrikes, Vahidi discussed Iran's nuclear position in an interview with state media. He said Iran would “do things it has not done previously” to defend itself, while adding that the country's position on nuclear weapons “has been stated with complete clarity in the past.”
The false quotation therefore did not represent a new declaration by Iran's military leadership, despite being presented that way by several accounts and media outlets.
The episode has underscored the risks of relying on viral social media claims during periods of heightened tensions, particularly when those claims concern nuclear weapons, military action and ongoing peace negotiations.

Japan’s defence minister will visit Canberra this week, the highest level engagement with Australia after controversy over Anthony Albanese’s comments about a gift of melons from prime minister Sanae Takaichi.
The defence minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, will meet his counterpart and deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on Tuesday, with discussions focused on Australia’s acquisition of Japan’s Mogami-class frigates and enhanced security cooperation.
Koizumi is considered a potential future prime minister of Japan. His father, Junichiro Koizumi, was prime minister from 2001 to 2006.
Koizumi’s visit comes after a week in which Albanese defended himself over comments made on the Bush Deep podcast, released last month.
He was discussing a pair of Japanese melons presented by Takaichi during a visit to Canberra earlier this year, and, while appearing to make hand gestures in front of his chest, said “she brought two, as you do”.
Host Nikki Osborne joked: “She came in looking like Pamela Anderson.”
Facing days of criticism from the opposition and in the media, Albanese has insisted his hand gestures and a comment about melons were misinterpreted and were not innuendo about breasts.
The opposition criticised Albanese for putting at risk close relations with one of Australia’s most important partners in Asia.
Public comments from Japan’s ambassador to Australia on Wednesday suggested Takaichi’s government wanted to avoid a diplomatic incident over the comments, which were initially not controversial but soon sparked strong criticism, including by a former envoy to Australia.
Japan’s government refrained from public comments on the issue until Wednesday, when its current ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki released a statement not raising any further issue with Albanese’s conduct.
Suzuki noted Takaichi had visited Australia in May – shortly before the interview in question – and had been hosted for dinner by Albanese “in a very relaxed atmosphere, and we believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders”.
Albanese had earlier apologised for comments about Australian signer Kylie Minogue made in the same appearance.
A Japanese diplomatic cable sent in July, and leaked during the controversy, blamed “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” and said Tokyo believed there was no “ill intention” in Albanese’s actions.
The visit comes as part of a five-day trip which will include a stop in India.
“Our relationship with Japan continues to go from strength to strength, and I look forward to welcoming my good friend, minister Koizumi back to Australia this week,” Marles told Guardian Australia.
“Together we will progress efforts to enhance defence cooperation and support our shared commitment to regional security, building on the joint statement announced by our prime ministers in May.
“This includes in the areas of co-developing and co-producing defence capabilities, advanced weapons testing, enhanced training and exercises, and increased information and intelligence cooperation.”
Takaichi has faced mounting political challenges, including on policies to help with the cost of living, and has seen sliding support in opinion polls in recent months.
Koizumi was criticised by China at the weekend for visiting the Yasukuni Shrine, dedicated to Japan’s war dead. Visits to the shrine by senior politicians are regularly criticised by Japan’s neighbours including China and South Korea, who suggest they are symbolic of a lack of remorse for Japan’s actions during the second world war.
In August last year, Labor agreed to buy Japan’s Mogami‑class frigates for the Royal Australian Navy.
Australia will spend $10bn over a decade to buy three of the frigates, with the first expected to be delivered in December 2029.

The protest by JPSC-JSSC aspirants in Ranchi entered its 24th day on Monday, with four student protesters continuing their hunger strike ahead of a fresh round of talks with the Jharkhand government. Chief Minister Hemant Soren-led Jharkhand government invited th protesting job aspirants protesting for a fresh rounds of talks on Monday. The development came a day after JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch — which is spearheading the protest — announced that its members would gherao chief minister Hemant Soren’s residence on August 20, demanding his resignation. The decision to invite the students for the 7th round of talks came after the sub-divisional officer and additional district magistrate, law and order held a meeting with the students at the protest site in Ranchi’s Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium. “The protesting students have been invited for a discussion on August 17 at 2 pm. They have been offered the option to participate in the talks accompanied by their legal advisors,” the statement issued by the Ranchi district administration said. Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto, who is on 16th day of hunger strike over alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC), on Sunday called for permanent reforms in the education system to ensure that future generations do not face similar hardships. In a post on X, Mahto said the government had called for talks on Monday and expressed hope that the dialogue would lead to a positive outcome. "On the 15th day of the hunger strike (Sunday), the situation is extremely critical and in its final phase. Yesterday, the government called for talks. We hope that this dialogue will yield a positive outcome and bring about such reforms in the education system that the coming generations will not have to endure the pain, struggle, and hardship that many young people are facing today", he said on X. Earlier, on Sunday, the protest by Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) aspirants entered its 23rd day, with student leaders announcing a gherao of Chief Minister Hemant Soren's residence on August 20. The students said they have agreed to attend a meeting with a government delegation at the State Guest House in Ranchi at 2 pm on Monday. Speaking to ANI, student protester Prem Nayak, who has been on hunger strike for 14 days, said that his health condition is deteriorating but urged that he will not withdraw from the agitation. "This is the 24th day of dharna and the 14th day of my hunger strike. My condition is serious, and my health is deteriorating. I don't feel I will live long, but I would rather die than step back. I will fight for this state and country till my last breath," Nayak said. He alleged that the government is not serious about the students' demands and is not ready for talks. "The government is not serious, not ready for talks. They are going around in circles. I would like to tell the government to think about us. Students are growing furious; you never know when this spark will turn into flames," he said. Ebola outbreak in DR Congo becomes deadliest in its history
- Published
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is now the deadliest in its history, according to public health officials.
A total of 2,325 people have been killed by the virus since it was declared on 15 May, surpassing the death toll of the country's 2018-2020 outbreak.
The outbreak was already the fastest growing on record, UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said last week, warning that "the epidemic is killing someone every 30 minutes".
There is currently no approved vaccine available for the Bundibugyo species that has caused the current epidemic but several are in development, including one based on technology used to develop the AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine.
DR Congo's Institute of Public Health on Sunday said it had recorded 4,945 confirmed cases, including 101 in the previous 24 hours.
Comparatively few cases have been identified outside the country: as of 12 August, 20 cases were confirmed in neighbouring Uganda, while two people were treated in Germany and one case was declared in France.
However, the pace of the virus's transmission in DR Congo, where it has spread to six of 26 provinces, has been described as "exceptional" by the World Health Organization.
According to Reuters, it took close to five months for the world's deadliest outbreak of 2014-2016 in West Africa to reach 1,000 fatalities. The current outbreak reached 2,000 deaths in three months, though researchers say it may have been spreading undetected since February.
The outbreak is the 17th to have emerged in DR Congo since Ebola was discovered 50 years ago. Years of conflict and a highly mobile population have added to the country's challenges in controlling the spread of the disease.
The WHO has said it hopes to reverse the spread of the disease within three months but warned that this meant bringing transmission under control and not ending the outbreak entirely.
Ebola is a rare but deadly viral disease and the Bundibugyo species is even rarer, with only two known prior outbreaks.
Symptoms of Ebola, which are similar to the flu or malaria, include fever, headache and tiredness, and can begin suddenly within two to 21 days of infection.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea can develop, leading to organ failure. Contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit causes the virus to spread.
The UK's medicines regulator, the MHRA, has given permission for the first human trials of a vaccine for Bundibugyo to go ahead.
The jab is being created by a team from the University of Oxford based on the same technology used in the Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid vaccine. Three other groups are also developing different vaccines for Bundibugyo.
The WHO is also sponsoring a separate clinical trial in DR Congo to see whether two existing antiviral therapies can improve survival rates.

Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.

“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Every summer evening, Gulshan follows the same routine. She washes the floor of her one-room home several times so it cools a little for her four children to sleep on. Last summer, the family saved enough to buy a desert cooler, which uses evaporation as a cheaper alternative to air conditioning.
The family uses the appliance cautiously to save on energy costs. But even when it is on, Gulshan, who does not use a surname, has to dampeneveryone’s clothes before sleeping. The 39-year-old and her children now have rashes and one has a skin infection from the wet cloth against their skin.
This summer, Gulshan started jotting down these coping strategies in a garmi khata, or heat registry. “I feel relieved that at least somebody might read my family’s experiences,” she says.
They are one of 40 households in Sunder Nagri, a slum in north-east Delhi, documenting their experiences of surviving the city’s increasingly longer and more frequent heatwaves.
Over the last few years, cities across India have begun drawing up heat action plans – agreements formulated by a municipality or district administration on how to prepare for and respond to extreme heat.
While some incorporate data such as satellite-derived land surface temperatures to identify heat hotspots, there are still significant gaps in information on people, making it difficult to understand how heat is experienced differently across communities.
Aravind Unni, an urban planner and researcher in Delhi, says: “Experiences of heat are vastly different depending on geography, income, occupation, gender, caste, class.
“While we have some meteorological data on heat, what’s absolutely missing is people, community – what they feel, what they experience.”
Most data collated in heat planning is usually just meteorological, such as air temperatures and heatwave thresholds.. The idea for the heat diaries was to “move beyond just the numbers”, says Nibedita Saha, a Greenpeace India researcher who worked on the project.
Aakiz Farooq, a senior campaigner at the group, says the team contemplated how best to encapsulate experiences and thought: “What if they become their own storytellers, they write their own evidence, they write their own testimonies?”
Arshi, 19, who lives in one room with five other family members, is a distance-learning student at Delhi University. She also works at home making decorative tassels for trucks.
She makes about 150 rupees (£1.17) working with her mother and sister for a day. “Sometimes I go to the college library just to sit in the air-conditioned space for a while. But I have to come back home so I can help my sister and mother,” she says. These experiences are part of Arshi’s diary.
The diaries, which ask about daily routines, work, home, mood and families, are intended to serve as comprehensive journals of residents’ daily lives.
Arshi’s small brick house is extremely humid, and while the temperatures are lower after rain, the combination of heat and humidity means everyone is sweating profusely.
The ambient air temperature insideis 29.3C (85F), but with relative humidity at 84.6%, the “feels-like” temperature is 36.3C (97F).
Raja, a 21-year-old street vendor, experiences temperatures as high as 45C during peak summer months as he sells vegetables from his pushcart. The fresh produce spoils quickly, leading to losses, and he has noticed a drastic drop in numbers of people on the street, which also reduces his income.
Every night, he returns to a home with limited ventilation and no cooling source beyond a ceiling fan. As the gap between day and night temperatures narrows year after year in Delhi, people in homes such as Raja’s get no respite, even after the sun sets. “I started sleeping out on the roof in May so I could feel some air,” he says.
Workers such as Raja, Unni says, could be better protected by public policy if the state knew of their experiences at a micro-level and establish systems to provide compensation.
When Sunder Nagri’s residents set out to map heat indices within their neighbourhood, they found that some streets, including where Raja sells vegetables, reflected temperatures on the ground of more than 54C (129F). The residents are attempting to find pragmatic solutions, such as shade, water sources or increased greenery.
This summer, satellite analysis found striking differences across Delhi. For instance, an analysis by the news magazine India Today found an average land-surface temperature of nearly 44C in the south-west district of Mahipalpur, by the airport, compared with about 37C just 2 miles (3km) away in the leafy, upmarket suburb of Vasant Kunj.
Unni feels the diaries and community heat mapping can help form urban resilience policy, but says a big stumbling block is that “Indian cities do not have the administrative capacity or infrastructure to have decentralised action”.
The diaries have now been submitted to India’s National Human Rights Commission, urging it to recognise extreme heat as a human rights issue and recommend measures to protect people.
Farooq says the team also plans to share the testimonies with ministries, policymakers and MPs to push for more targeted measures to protect people from extreme heat.
He says they are also working to develop the testimonies into evidence of impacts and injuries that could be used for lawsuits to increase accountability, given the supreme court’s 2024 ruling that protection from the most adverse impacts of the climate crisis forms part of the right to life.
On 4 August, India’s government added heatwaves to the list of nationally notified disasters, allowing states to access emergency relief funds.
Unni and Farooq say it “would be ideal” if the decision meant funds could support local action guided by community participation.
Arshi also feels more hopeful after the new guidelines. “Even if the government sees something as small as our rising medical and electricity costs and tries to help with that, it would feel like a win for me. At least they would have seen what we are going through,” she says.

You might want to skip Newegg's GPU trade-in program
The convenience may be worth it for some.
Trading in old hardware makes upgrading easy, but selling your old GPU yourself could leave considerably more money in your pocket.
Newegg's GPU Trade-In program makes upgrading surprisingly painless. Choose an eligible replacement, tell Newegg what old components you have, complete your purchase and the retailer will send you a prepaid UPS label to send your outdated hardware back. Once your trade-in passes inspection, the agreed credit amount is refunded to your original payment method. There is, however, a pretty sizable convenience fee hiding in those numbers.
Those trade-in values can fall well short of what comparable components have recently fetched on eBay, which poses a rather obvious question: How much is it actually worth to avoid the hassle of selling your GPU, CPU or memory yourself?
Selling it yourself could leave you with a lot more money
That difference is hard to ignore with the RTX 2060 Super in particular. The 8GB card is listed at $60 on Newegg, and a working Zotac RTX 2060 Super sold on eBay for $161.99 on July 13. An Asus Prime RTX 5070 sold for $565 on June 4 compared to Newegg's $400 trade-in, while an RTX 3080 Ti Founders Edition fetched $500 on June 26. Newegg's offer is only $380.
Those are individual sales, of course. GPU prices vary by manufacturer, condition, accessories and plain old buyer demand, while selling through eBay also means dealing with marketplace fees and potentially paying for shipping.
Still, there's plenty of breathing room in some of those gaps. That RTX 2060 Super sold for $101.99 more than Newegg's offer before marketplace fees entered the picture. That's a fairly steep price to pay for avoiding an eBay listing. Newegg says it may change its trade-in offers based on market conditions, but the company doesn't say how those values are calculated against prices in the broader used-component market.
Newegg is really just selling convenience
To be fair, convenience is where the program makes its case. Newegg handles the shipping with a prepaid UPS label, gives customers 14 days to send their old component and returns rejected hardware without charging for return shipping.
The inspection is thorough, too. Newegg checks the submitted model and serial number, looks at physical damage, rust or corrosion, fan and port functionality, operating temperatures, noise levels and benchmark performance before accepting a trade-in. Once you've shipped your item to Newegg, the trade-in can no longer be canceled. Inspection takes 10 to 15 business days, and it's another three to five days for the credit.
There's another limitation worth knowing: You can't simply send Newegg an old GPU, CPU or memory and ask for cash. A trade-in has to accompany an eligible purchase, such as another component or qualifying gaming PC, and the replacement product must cost more than the trade-in offer.
Traded-in graphics cards and other electronics can also feed into Newegg Refreshed, the retailer's refurbished-electronics program where inspected hardware is resold.

- The claim that a Muslim family living in the Middle East recently bought one of the biggest Bible-producing publishers in the world is unproven.
- The rumor stems from a video published in early August 2026, in which California-based author and pastor Jack Hibbs urges his viewers to quickly buy physical Bibles, alleging "a Muslim family in the Middle East just bought one of the biggest Bible-producing publishers in the world." He did not mention the purported company's name.
- As of this writing, we did not yet uncover evidence to confirm or debunk this rumor.
- Snopes contacted Hibbs to ask for evidence substantiating his claim. We did not receive a response within several days but will update this article if further information becomes available.
- We also reached out by email to numerous Bible publishers and sellers to inquire if they were aware of the sale of a major company. As of this writing, we had not received any responses substantiating the rumor.
For example, on Aug. 6, a TikTok user posted (archived) the clip with the onscreen caption, "Get your Bibles NOW."
The man speaking in the video urges viewers to quickly purchase a physical Bible, apparently over fears of the Muslim family who allegedly purchased the publisher altering the Christian text in favor of Islam. He uses the words "just bought," suggesting the purchase occurred recently:
Just make sure you own an actual Bible. Can you do it kind of quick, please? I'm not going to mention the name right now cause I don't want to get sued. But a Muslim family in the Middle East just bought one of the biggest Bible-producing publishers in the world. Why? Why would Muslims buy a Bible-producing company? They pu-, they, hmm. My point is this, will you buy a Bible right away so nobody can change the Bible?
One Facebook user posted a video asking (archived), "Breaking news! Christians, I need your help with this one! Is this rumor true?!" A different Facebook user also requested (archived) confirmation of the truth, as did a Snopes reader who emailed us to ask, "Did a Muslim family buy a Bible publishing company in order to subvert the Bible or limit access?"
In sum, our investigation has yet to uncover evidence confirming or debunking the claim that a Muslim family in the Middle East bought a major Bible-producing publisher. As such, we've left this article unrated until we learn more.
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo and Google failed to locate any news media outlets, including Christian or political publications, reporting on the matter. Those searches did, however, find the name of the man speaking in the clip.
The video features author Jack Hibbs, who serves as the senior and founding pastor of Calvary Chapel Chino Hills in Chino, California, and founder of the faith-based Real Life Network. The clip originated from the Aug. 6 episode (archived) of Hibbs' YouTube podcast, "Real Life with Jack Hibbs."
We emailed Hibbs at two different email addresses, reached out via a contact form on his church's website and left a message with his assistant at the church, asking for information that might allow us to confirm the claim. We did not receive a response within several days but will update this article if we receive further information.
Researching the rumor
In the video, Hibbs claims a Muslim family recently bought "one of the biggest Bible-producing publishers in the world" and urges his viewers to quickly buy physical Bibles.

Cambridge University Press spokesperson Matt Midgley told Snopes via email, "Cambridge University Press & Assessment is part of the University of Cambridge. We couldn't comment on any other publisher." Midgley did not provide additional details related to Cambridge's publishing operation.
A Humble Lamb spokesperson emailed, "Humble Lamb is a Christian family owned and family run business located in Kentucky. Humble Lamb's sole owner is the founder Daniel Arroyo, since the beginning in 2017. We also do not know of any Bible publishers being owned by Middle Eastern Muslim families."
Lifeway Christian Resources spokesperson Carol Pipes said via email, "We have no knowledge of this happening with any Bible publisher in the industry. I also reached out to our B&H team," referencing the "trade book arm of Lifeway," adding that "they were not aware of this happening either."

As Americans cook their vegetables to at least 158°F to kill a diarrheal parasite that has sickened over 24,000 people and killed two this summer, one US Senator is turning up the heat on Health Secretary Robert F. Kenney Jr. over the government’s “calamitous response” to the record outbreak.
In a letter sent Thursday, Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called the federal response to the Cyclospora outbreak “botched” and “marred by missteps.” She pointedly questioned whether corruption and incompetence within the Trump administration and its clear ties to Taylor Farms—the mammoth produce distributer that sold Mexican-grown iceberg lettuce linked to the outbreak—played a role in the federal government’s failures.
“[P]olitical contributions and direct White House lobbying from Taylor Farms… raise urgent questions about the role this influence-peddling may have played in loosening federal food safety oversight and hampering the federal government’s response to the outbreak,” Warren wrote in the letter.
As Ars Technica has previously reported, Taylor Farms made a $1 million donation to a Trump-backing super PAC, MAGA, Inc, in March 2025. That donation came just days after the Food and Drug Administration announced it was delaying implementing a food traceability rule that would have made it easier to trace and respond to outbreaks, like the Cyclospora outbreak.
Warren’s letter noted other donations to Trump-aligned entities from Taylor Farms and said the contributions totaled into the millions. She further pointed out that Taylor Farms has hired former Trump White House official Trent Morse to lobby on behalf of the company. Morse reportedly brokered a direct call between Taylor Farms and the White House after the FDA had linked the company’s lettuce to the outbreak. In the call, Taylor Farms allegedly made an “urgent plea” to delay a recall of the tainted lettuce.
Clear delay
Warren also noted a significant lingering question about the federal government’s response. Local media outlets reported that Taco Bell restaurants in Michigan and nearby states began pulling iceberg lettuce from their menus as early as July 7. Notices at the restaurant said they were unable to sell the produce “due to a nationwide recall.” But at the time, no recall had been reported by federal agencies.

Seventy years ago, the physicists Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines took a custom-built 10-ton detector, surrounded it with thick lead walls and wet sandbags, and placed it near a powerful nuclear reactor at the Savannah River Plant in South Carolina. They called the experiment Project Poltergeist, designed as it was to catch a ghost.
More than a quarter of a century before, physicists had been puzzling over why energy appeared to be lost during a radioactive process called beta decay. Something was missing, and there was no known physics to explain it. Then in 1930, the Austrian physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed a radical solution: A virtually undetectable particle was silently carrying the missing energy away. “I have done a terrible thing,” Pauli told a friend. “I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected.” It would come to be known as the neutrino. Having almost no mass and no charge, these particles can pass through Earth and everything on it, including our bodies, virtually unimpeded.
The massive device that Cowan and Reines deployed in early 1956 was meant to find what Pauli thought was impossible. That June, the pair of physicists from the Los Alamos National Laboratory sent Pauli a telegram: “We are happy to inform you that we have definitely detected neutrinos.”
Attention then shifted to a broader question. If nuclear reactions produce neutrinos, could we use them to peer at the nuclear fireworks inside stars, including the sun? This presented a huge challenge: How can you possibly catch particles shooting from distant stars if these particles can pass through almost anything undetected? The suspicion was that detecting a particle that rarely collides with matter requires a vast amount of matter for it to collide with. Moreover, the matter would have to be shielded from the noise of other forms of radiation. So the answer scientists came up with was to build some of the biggest, deepest, and most exotic experimental traps in scientific history … and then wait.
In the 1960s, Raymond Davis Jr. and colleagues at Brookhaven National Laboratory placed a tank 1.5 kilometers underground in the Homestake mine in South Dakota and filled it with nearly 400,000 liters of a chlorine-based cleaning fluid called perchloroethylene. On the rare occasion that a passing neutrino struck a chlorine nucleus, it would be transformed into a radioactive form of argon that could be detected and counted. The experiment, which would run for 25 years, found just one-third the number of neutrinos coming from the sun that had been predicted in theoretical models. This became known as the solar neutrino problem.
Decades passed before it was solved—by yet more massive experiments. Deep in the Kamioka mine in Japan, Masatoshi Koshiba built a different kind of detector called Kamiokande, which used 3 million liters of ultrapure water. In this setup, neutrinos occasionally interact with atomic nuclei in the water. The interaction creates an electron that moves so fast, it generates a flash of what’s called Cherenkov light. This light gets picked up by detectors.
Kamiokande and Koshiba confirmed Davis’ shortfall, and a second, even larger detector, Super-Kamiokande, as well as Canada’s Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, explained the discrepancy. Neutrinos come in three different “flavors” (electron, muon, and tau) and can oscillate, or switch, between them. To do so, neutrinos must have mass, which the laws of physics failed (and still fail) to predict.
Newer neutrino detectors continue the tradition of grand ambitions and surprising results. The IceCube Neutrino Observatory below the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station uses Antarctic ice instead of water. It has developed a map of the Milky Way made up only of neutrinos and traced these high-energy cosmic particles back to active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes. On the floor of the Mediterranean Sea, the Cubic Kilometer Neutrino Telescope (KM3NET) has detected the highest-energy cosmic neutrino on record. Its source remains unknown.
Neutrino oscillations, and the myriad mysteries they give rise to, have driven the development of the newest wave of detectors. China’s Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) launched in 2025; initial data published in June 2026 provided the most precise measurements of neutrino oscillation reported to date. Japan’s Hyper-Kamiokande (Hyper-K) and the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) in the American Midwest are both expected to begin operation later this decade.
Because of these and other audacious experiments, the particle that Pauli was sure could never be caught has slowly been revealing its secrets. The recipe for discovery hasn’t changed in seven decades: Think big, go deep, and summon patience.

The Labor government has pledged a new single-service opt-out register for gambling ads - an idea similar to the Do Not Call register for spam calls - as part of amendments to its wagering ad bill, as well as restrictions on inducements and limiting commissions for agents.
Communications minister Anika Wells has also confirmed gambling companies will face a new levy to pay for the register, a beefed-up measure to curb wagering ads, after concerns were raised through a Senate inquiry that Australians would struggle to find or complete individual opt-out options on each online service.
The measure falls short of calls from some, including Labor and Liberal MPs, for an “opt-in” model for gambling ads, or for a complete ban on online advertising.
The Albanese government’s gambling reforms are expected to proceed quickly through parliament this week, with Labor sources saying they hoped the changes contained in two separate bills would pass both houses before the end of Thursday. A Senate inquiry into the government’s bill will be tabled on Monday afternoon.
Despite Labor’s hopes of passing its gambling legislation this week, the Coalition has not yet publicly committed to supporting the package.
While a further raft of amendments to the bill are likely to outlined tomorrow, Wells on Monday introduced a third bill setting out some changes the government proposes to make to its own legislation.
The bill’s explanatory memorandum says the government’s plans include “restricting the use of inducements by licensed interactive wagering service providers”, as well as plans to prohibit “inducement-based direct marketing and social media advertising to certain customers, restricts attempts to obtain consent to receive such marketing, prohibits certain commission-based referral arrangements”.
“The government has listened carefully to the evidence presented during the recent Senate inquiry and through ongoing stakeholder engagement. We are particularly concerned by evidence about wagering inducements and the role these practices can play in encouraging gambling and exacerbating gambling-related harm,” Wells told parliament in introducing the new bill.
A major change contained in the third bill is a new “Wagering Advertising Opt-out Register”. While neither Wells’ speech nor the explanatory memorandum explains exactly how this would work, the explanation says it would be “a single mechanism through which individuals may opt out of receiving wagering advertising from online content service providers”.
Labor’s initial bill had stopped short of enacting a full ban on wagering ads online, as recommended by Peta Murphy’s landmark 2023 parliamentary report, in favour of establishing a “triple lock” system for ads to be shown online; that online ads could only be shown to users who are logged-in and aged over 18, and provided with an opt-out feature.
But gambling harm advocates and critics of Labor’s bill had criticised this system, saying existing opt-out features on streaming services or social media platforms were often hard to find online, and that only a tiny percentage of users had made use of those features.
The government’s new proposal for a single opt-out register is a compromise to provide an easier avenue for opting out of ads, without enacting a full ban or switching to an opt-in.
Wells told parliament that the register would “provide Australians with a ‘one-stop shop’ to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms”, and be administered and established by the Australian Communications and Media Authority .
Guardian Australia is seeking information about how the register would operate.
“This Bill enables the ACMA to recover the costs of those activities through a levy imposed on licensed interactive wagering service providers. It is appropriate that the wagering industry, rather than taxpayers, bears the costs of regulating these activities,” Wells said.

Aid shortages and fears of starvation as Indonesia reels from deadly earthquake
- Published
Aid disruptions and aftershocks across the Indonesian island of Flores are fuelling fears among thousands of survivors who were displaced by a 7.7 magnitude earthquake on Saturday.
Refugees are sleeping outdoors through sweltering days and frigid nights for fear that more buildings may collapse. Tents set up amid the rubble of collapsed hospitals are serving as makeshift emergency rooms for injured patients. And as landslides sever access roads and supplies dwindle in several parts of the island, there are growing concerns about how much longer survivors can hold out.
At least 53 people were killed and some 5,000 displaced by the initial quake, which struck shortly before 06:00 Saturday (23:00 GMT Friday) at a depth of just 15km.
It is the country's deadliest earthquake since 2022, when hundreds of people were killed in West Java.
"We heard that medical assistance would be provided, but nothing has arrived yet," Rista Mari, a public relations officer at the Ruteng Regional General Hospital in Manggarai Regency, told the BBC. "We hope that assistance will arrive soon."
Early data from Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency indicates that more than 1,000 houses have been damaged, along with dozens of health facilities, schools and government offices.
But the full scale of the disaster is still being uncovered.
In Flores' westernmost town of Labuan Bajo, the gateway to Komodo National Park and one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations, many survivors have been sleeping outdoors, fearful that if the tremors continue they might be crushed in their sleep.
"The shaking was very scary. My house almost collapsed," said one farmer named Anastasia Imad, from a green emergency tent erected next to her damaged home. "We were worried that the aftershocks would collapse the house while we were sleeping."
Herry Kabut, editor-in-chief of local publication Floresa Media, told the BBC that "each resident has set up their own evacuation post" amid blackouts, landslides and roadblocks.
"So far, many basic necessities such as [basic foodstuffs] and clean water are in great demand," he said. "People have no idea where to evacuate. There's been no government advice. Many have fled to the hills and are starving."
Health services across the island have similarly been forced to move outside and set up emergency tents due to damaged facilities. Ruteng Regional General Hospital's operating room, delivery room, pharmacy, and laboratory were all rendered defunct after the building's roof collapsed.
Elsewhere, in Ngada Regency, local resident Charles Abar told the BBC that health facilities and equipment had been severely damaged and that, as of Sunday night, no medical assistance had arrived.
He believes the government's response hasn't been swift enough.
"I think facilities like emergency tents need to be provided immediately, but I also see that district and regional governments are struggling due to budget constraints, limited supplies, and so on," he said.
Meanwhile, he added, villages have been cut off from aid and displaced people whose homes were damaged or destroyed have been forced to seek higher ground, as hundreds of aftershocks continue to rattle the island.
"The community is still traumatised," he stressed.
Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates.
On Sunday night, rescuers successfully reached a village on Palue Island, just north of Flores's mainland, that had been cut off for nearly two full days after the initial quake.
Rescuers were only able to reach Nitung Village after a two-hour overland journey from the coast.
"Our challenge was the road, which was still prone to landslides," said Sikka Deputy Police Chief Commissioner Marselus Yugo Amboro, who led the rescue mission. "It was a life-threatening route."
Yugo said hundreds of homes in Nitung Village were severely damaged by the earthquake, and that residents had been sheltering in makeshift shelters. Electricity and communication lines were completely cut off following the earthquake, he added.
"They haven't received aid yet because Nitung Village was isolated for nearly two days after the quake," he said, noting that efforts were underway to rush aid to the survivors.
"This is likely the village in Sikka Regency that suffered the worst damage from the earthquake."

Extreme heat, humidity, cold weather and changes in routine can make periods harder to manage. But persistent changes in cycle length, bleeding or pain should not simply be blamed on the weather; medical attention should be sought
A period arriving a few days earlier or later than expected can be unsettling, particularly during a heatwave, a spell of heavy rain or a sudden change in routine. The menstrual cycle is primarily regulated by hormonal signals between the brain and ovaries. Weather does not directly control menstruation, but extreme conditions can place physical stress on the body and affect sleep, hydration, physical activity, appetite and stress levels. These changes may, in turn, affect ovulation and the symptoms experienced around a period.
How it works
Sandhya Vasan, director and senior consultant, gynecology, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, says extreme weather can act as a physiological stressor. The body’s stress response involves hormones such as cortisol, which can affect the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis that regulates ovulation and menstruation. If this hormonal signalling is disrupted, ovulation may be delayed, occur earlier or, in some cases, be skipped, resulting in a longer, shorter or irregular cycle.
The evidence linking weather directly to menstrual changes, however, remains limited. Much of the effect may come from the changes that extreme weather brings to everyday life rather than from temperature itself.
Heat can amplify symptoms
Extreme heat can make an already uncomfortable period harder to manage. Dehydration, fatigue and poor sleep can add to the physical stress of menstruation and may make cramps, headaches, dizziness and premenstrual symptoms more noticeable.
P.M. Gopinath, director of reproductive medicine, Kauvery Hospital, Vadapalani, Chennai, says heat causes blood vessels to dilate as the body attempts to lose heat. At the same time, sweating leads to fluid and electrolyte loss. Together with heat-related fatigue and disturbed sleep, these changes can make menstrual symptoms feel more intense.
Pavithra Ramakrishnan, consultant, obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, OMR, Chennai, says some women may notice heavier or lighter bleeding, fatigue and headaches during extreme heat. Dehydration and physical stress can also affect the timing of ovulation, potentially shifting the next period.
However, a change in bleeding should not automatically be considered a response to temperature. Persistent or significant changes require assessment for other causes.
Some women may be more vulnerable to the effects of extreme weather. These include adolescents whose cycles are still becoming regular, women with PMOS (previously PCOS) or thyroid disorders, athletes, outdoor workers and those with limited access to water and rest. Women approaching perimenopause, or those prone to migraines or low blood pressure, may also find symptoms more difficult to manage.
Cold weather effects
The relationship between cold weather and menstruation is less clear. Cold can cause blood vessels to constrict and muscles to tighten, which may make cramps feel worse for some women. Reduced physical activity during colder weather can also contribute to discomfort.
Heavy rain and flooding create a different menstrual health concern. When transport is disrupted or access to toilets, clean water and menstrual products is limited, maintaining menstrual hygiene becomes more difficult. The problem is therefore not only physical discomfort but also access to basic facilities needed to manage menstruation safely.
Humidity and hygiene
Hot and humid conditions can also increase sweat and moisture around the genital area. This can contribute to irritation, chafing and skin infections, particularly when tight synthetic clothing or damp clothes are worn for long periods.
Dr. Gopinath recommends changing menstrual products regularly, wearing breathable cotton underwear and keeping the area clean and dry. Scented products that can irritate sensitive skin should be avoided. Cloth pads should be washed thoroughly and dried completely before reuse.
Managing periods
Managing the effects of extreme weather largely involves reducing the additional physical stress on the body.
Adequate fluid intake is important, particularly during hot and humid weather. There is no single amount of water that everyone needs each day; requirements vary with temperature, physical activity and individual health. Water-rich foods such as cucumber, watermelon and citrus fruits can also contribute to fluid intake.
A balanced diet, including iron-rich foods, can help maintain energy levels, particularly for women who have heavy menstrual bleeding. Light physical activity such as walking, stretching or yoga may help with cramps. During extreme heat, strenuous exercise can be shifted to cooler parts of the day, with adequate rest and fluids.
Keeping a menstrual calendar can help distinguish an occasional change from a persistent pattern. Recording the dates of periods, duration of bleeding, flow and associated symptoms can also provide useful information during a medical consultation.
When to seek help
The most important distinction is between a temporary change during extreme weather and a persistent menstrual problem.
A period that is slightly early or late after a period of heat, poor sleep or disrupted routine may not indicate an underlying disorder. But repeated irregularity should not be explained away as a weather-related effect.
Doctors recommend medical evaluation if cycles remain irregular for about three cycles, bleeding becomes unusually heavy or pain is severe. Periods lasting more than seven days, fainting, significant dehydration, fever or foul-smelling discharge also warrant medical attention. Severe pain that does not improve with usual measures should not be ignored.
Conditions such as PMOS (previously PCOS) and thyroid disorders can cause irregular periods and abnormal ovulation independently of weather. If such conditions are suspected, appropriate evaluation and treatment may be needed.
Weather can therefore influence menstrual health, particularly by adding physical stress or worsening existing symptoms. But it should not become an easy explanation for persistent changes that warrant medical attention.

Keeper Bihina stars as Cameroon upset Morocco to make Wafcon final
- Published
Michaely Bihina was the heroine as the Cameroon goalkeeper saved an extra-time penalty and three more spot-kicks in a shootout to send her side though to the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations final at the expense of host nation Morocco.
The 22-year-old pushed away Fatima Tagnaout's attempt from 12 yards in the 118th minute to ensure the game in Rabat finished 0-0 after 120 minutes.
Bihina then brilliantly kept out efforts from Kenza Chapelle, Maryame Atiq and Sakina Ouzraoui to leave the Moulay Hassan Stadium in stunned silence.
Teenage Cameroon defender Myriam Nyadjou held her nerve to secure a 3-1 win on penalties for the Central Africans.
The Indomitable Lionesses will face Malawi in Sunday's final (19:00 GMT) after the southern Africans beat Algeria 3-1 earlier on Wednesday.
Cameroon's run to the final is all the more remarkable given they were knocked out in qualifying and only progressed to the finals on the strength of their world ranking after the Confederation of African Football decided to expand the tournament to 16 teams midway through the preliminary process.
Morocco suffer heartbreak again
While the first Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) semi-final was littered with chances and incident, the late game in the capital was a far tighter affair.
Morocco created little to reflect their dominance of the ball against an organised and disciplined Cameroon side who grew in confidence in the latter stages of the second half.
The Atlas Lionesses came close to an opener in the 14th minute when Sanaa Mssoudy diverted Hanane Ait El Haj's right-wing cross against the right-hand upright, and the forward also thrashed into the side-netting on the hour mark.
A flurry of late chances came at the end of regulation time, with Imane Saoud shooting straight at Bihina, Mssoudy heading wide and Michaela Abam firing over the Morocco bar.
Abam then had a shot blocked towards the end of the first period of extra time and Morocco defender Atiq headed over in the second half.
The match's key incident came right at the end of extra time when Morocco were presented with a glorious chance to win the tie following a video assistant referee (VAR) review, with Togolese official Vincentia Amedome deciding Nyadjou had caught Ouzraoui in the face with her arm.
Ait El Haj had converted from the spot in the quarter-final win over South Africa but substitute Tagnaout assumed responsibilities and the winger's tame left-footed effort was palmed away by Bihina.
There was more to come from the Cameroon keeper, who joined Portuguese giants Benfica in February and had previously made a remarkable nine stops in her side's quarter-final upset against 10-time champions Nigeria.
Chapelle put her effort too close to Bihina but two stunning stops followed to deny Atiq and Ouzraoui.
Khadija Er-Rmichi had kept her side in the shootout by saving an effort from Grace Mendoua, but the Morocco keeper had little answer to Bihina's heroics.
A semi-final defeat comes as a big blow to Morocco, who have invested heavily in football in recent years and hired Spain's Women's World Cup winning manager Jorge Vilda in an attempt to claim a maiden continental crown.
The Atlas Lionesses were runners-up in 2022 and reached the final of the delayed 2024 Wafcon last July, but threw away a 2-0 half-time lead against Nigeria and were forced to settle for second place again.
Cameroon, meanwhile, return to the final for the first time since losing to Nigeria as tournament hosts in 2016.
The Indomitable Lionesses have lost three previous finals and coach Valentine Nguele, who only took charge in June, will need to nullify the threat of the Chawinga sisters Tabitha and Temwa when her side come up against Malawi on Sunday.
Whoever comes out on top, it will be a new name on the trophy.
On Thursday Ivory Coast take on Ghana (17:00 GMT) and Nigeria meet South Africa (20:00 GMT) in African play-offs for the chance to go into an inter-continental qualifier for the 2027 Fifa Women's World Cup.

Turn on these settings to protect your Android phone from theft
Google has added some smart theft-detection features to Android in recent years.
For years, Android anti-theft protection was more reactionary than proactive. Users are all too familiar with traditional warnings and protocols, like shielding your phone when entering your PIN, utilizing location services and avoiding easily guessed passwords. Fortunately, anti-theft tools are finally getting better at preventing theft with the help of AI and Google's built-in Theft Protection suite.
If your phone is snatched out of your hand, for instance, new motion-sensing theft detection will quickly lock it down. If a thief kills your connection by pulling your SIM card or switching to Airplane Mode, the Offline Device Lock feature triggers a countdown, locking the screen in short order. These are nifty new features that avoid annoying false positives with usage limitations and active use checks.
Even better, you don't have to dig deep into your device settings to find and activate theft protection measures. As long as your device is running Android 10 or newer, the feature is bundled into Google Play Services. Keep in mind that some entry-level or budget smartphones running Android Go Edition with low RAM, Android tablets and devices lacking the full range of Google Play Services may not have some or all of Google's security suite features.
How to Enable Anti-Theft Features On Android?
The primary settings to look for are under Google's Theft Protection menu. Settings menus aren't universal with Android phones, so there may be a degree of variation between devices. For Samsung users, the order is typically Settings → Security and Privacy → Lost Device Protection → Theft Protection.
Google Pixel phones are similar, but slightly different: Settings → Security & Privacy → Device Unlock → Theft Protection. The most prominent feature is Theft Detection Lock, and it's best to start there. This uses motion and sudden disconnection indicators (like your phone being snatched and moved quickly) to lock down your phone screen automatically. After you turn it on and confirm, your device will now respond to aggressive or sudden movement.
Next, enable Offline Device Lock so your screen stays protected if a thief disables your mobile data or Wi-Fi by switching Airplane Mode on. The lock will kick in shortly after disconnect and doesn't require a local connection to do so. Last but not least, set up Remote Lock. This lets you lock your phone from anywhere by visiting android.com/lock, entering your phone number and following the prompts. Google's Find Hub app is no longer your sole fallback option, and Remote Lock works even if the thief moves the phone to another network.
How Can You Prevent Thieves from Turning Off Your Device?
You'll never fully take advantage of the Theft Protection features if you don't use a PIN, biometrics and a more complicated password than your first name. Besides, Google explicitly requires a screen lock for Identity Check and other device-protection tools, so you may as well set it up properly. On Pixels and newer Android phones, Identity Check can periodically re-verify using your biometrics or PIN, especially when you're off your regular beaten path and away from work or home.
Enable Theft Detection Lock and Offline Device Lock so your phone auto-locks and remains that way, even if the thief yanks it offline. If they try to power it down or keep it in Airplane Mode, your data remains secure behind the screen lock, completely shielded. On Samsung Galaxy phones, there is a dedicated Theft Protection page that ties into Samsung's own lost-device tools as well.
Make sure Remote Lock is enabled and your phone number is verified, so you can lock your phone down from any browser the moment you realize your phone is gone and you didn't leave it on top of the car or inside the refrigerator. Hey, it happens.
